A Chester-le-Street character was bragging about the good appearance of a coat which had recently come into his possession. After setting forth all its superior quali- ties, he clinched the matter by bursting out :—" Man, it's a grand coat; areal Melton Mowbray !" ' "That man just going out has a very interesting his- tory," said Jones. " Indeed !" said -Jenkins, looking _

backward: "Would you mind telling Me what it is?" " • Macaulay's History of England; " replied Jones as he departed hastly ; "he's just bought it." A tight place: The bar ropm. A handicap: The Turkish fez. Too often left: The right path. A good boarder: The carpenter. Cat and came again: Whiskers. The world's fair: Lovely woman. There are millions in . _ ..
it: Poverty. Hooks a-nd I's: The fisherman's story. Before the footlights: Boots and shoes. P. stitch in
time: The clock U.n a stocking. Quick, the comedian, once played for :la's benefit Richard 111. His intention was to have acted with

becoming seriousness, but the public, vnticipaing a burlesque, would be satisfied with nothing else. When he came to the famous line, "A horse! a horse !ny kingdom for a horse !" he convu`sed the hovso by ado- jug, quietly, " Aed if you can't get ajtorss bring a jack- ass."

A story is told of a certain Mayor of Cork who headed - a deputation to the late Emperor of the French, and commenced an oration to his Majesty in which he con- ceived to be the French tongue. "Pardon me" said the Emperor, after he had listened to the speech with much patience. "English I know fairly well; but, I regret to say, I have never had an opportunity of studying the Irish language !" An absurd blunder is related in Torn Moore's "Diary" about John Kemble. He was performing one of his favourite parts at some country theatre, and was inter- rupted from time to time by the squalling of a child in the gallery, until at length, angered by this rival per- formance, Kemble walked with solemn steps to the front of the stage, and, addressing the audience in his most tragic tones, said, "Ladies and gentleman, unless the play is stopped, the child cannot possibly go on !" ALICE'S JOKE. "Dees it hurt, my dear papa, to have a mustache?" Said sweet little Alice one day, As her speller she closed and gazed in my face In a puzzled, inquisitive way. " Why no," I responded, caressing her hair; Why utterance to such-a question make?" "Well, you see," she replied, in an innocent way, "In one way the word spells must-ache." It seems hi be the ambition of all young wives to look *ell when any one calls. A young bride heard a ring at the front door. The maid was out, and she rushed up- stairs to tidy a little before admitting the caller. There was a moment of lightning work before the dressing- table. Quicker than it takes to tell it a ribbon was fastened to her throat, a flower stabbed into her hair, a flash of powder on her face, and she was at the door— all smiles and blushes. The "gentleman" said he had the cheapest clothes props that could be bought for isioney. / A good story is told concerning the late Rev. W. Barnes, the Dorsetshire poet, which will interest spelling reformers :—" One day he went into a village school where a little boy and girl were sitting together. The girl was crying, and when he asked the reason, she said that Johnny had had the word ' Psalm ' to write in his copybook. and,' she said, with a fresh burst of the tears, 'he ha' scrope out the "P" with his elbow!' Then Johnny fired up, and said. 'What if I did scrope of en I out? He didn't spell naught, and what was the good‘of I en?'"

A WESTERN CREST.—The people who invent heraldic crests and mottoes are finding plenty to do now-a-days. The other day a man, who "recently made a stake" in a western mine, called at one of their establishments, and said, "The girls want some sort of a motter, or crest, as they call it, to put on their letter paper. I think it's all dozg,oned foolishness, but 's long as they want it they must have it. So I want you to fix up one o' yer most expensive crests, like what them English daoks and counts have, and send the bill to me. What mottor Well, I don't care much. 'I ain't pretty, but I get there all the same,' would suit me all right. Just throw it into Latin or Greek, and twine it around the crest." A JAPANESE "SPREE."—They are telling in Boston of two or three Japanese students of rank who have been in the habit of dining each Sunday at the residence of one of the solid citizens of the Hub. On a recent Sun- day one was absent, and when the host asked why, ono of the guests said solemnly, "Oh, he cannot come, he very, very dissipated!" The host thought it best not to make any further inquiry at the time, but after the meal he ventured to ask the same young man in pri- vate—" You say Mr. Nim Shi is not well 2" "No; :he is not well—he very dissipated." "He hasn't been drinking?" "Oh, no. no! He no drunk." "Not gam- bling ? " "No. no! He no gamble." "May I ask what he has been doing then 2" "Oh, he very dissipated. He cat spongee cake allee time—he all broke up now." PRINTERS' BLUNDERS.— Printers' blunders are not confined to England. Here is ample proof in a clipping from the Natal Mercury :—"There was an absurd printer's error in my columns last week—writes 'Man in the Moon '—the word 'woman' being:substituted for 'worm.' Think of ! The following has reference thereto:— Wear Man,—Your compositor's blunder of woman' for worm ' in Saturday's Mercury afforded, such a hearty I laugh that we must condone the offence. I never heard of a woman being caught with a rod, though it is said that Russian peasants present their future lords at the time of marriage with a whip to chastise them when disobedient in their future oath through life. Neither is 'dropping a line' to a lady when popping the question considered to be as good form as a personal application. As regards myself, in my fishing !days, I never even caught one of Kingsley's water babies or a mermaid, who is only half a woman. A propos of strange captures in the water, a very young friend of mine, aged six, went fishing some time back for the first time with his papa and a friend. What is the matter with Charley.' asked the friend. 'He is running here full tilt, and has thrown down his rod." What is 5t Charley; have you caught a fish?' Charley, with an awe-struck voice: 'No, papa, not a fish, but—but I really think I have caught the devil" A small eel was wriggling at the end of the hook, which resembled the Serpent in Eden, in his picture Bible !—Yours ever, H. 8."

" Air.—Cavalier." 'T was a dark cloudy night, and the moon gave no kilt, And the stars were all put in the shade, When a coal heaver named Mac, in a new fantail hat, Went courting his charming dustmaid. With his heart in a lame, he went down Drury-lane, And a very short pipe smoked he, But this gay coal heaver thought himself no small beer, For I'm a good looking covey. cry'd he. I'm a good looking, 84c. Be cock'd up his eye, at the house he drew nigh, Determined he would'nt be baulked; At the door he did knock, but found it wern't lock'd, So into the passage he waiked. Then upstairs went Mac, to the second floorlack, But no one.at home found he. What is this in her room, 'tis an old chummey's broom, And it never belonged to me.
This broom, Sze. You'd have thought, in despair, he'd have torn out his

hair, Or jumped off a three legged stool,. With a rope round his neck, just to give it a stretch, But Mac wasn't quite such a fool. Mac sensible still, of luve he'd his fill, And as homeward he rolled said he, When a lady so soon jumps over a broom, She may go to the devil for me.
She may go, &e.

"THINK OF YOUR HEAD IN THE MORNING." Tom Jennings, who never could drinking avoid, Tho' vows he was always a-making, For after each bout he was ever annoyed By nervousness and a headaching. Going out to a party one evening last week, MS wife said to him as a warning, " New be careful, dear Thomas 4 and mind what you drink, And think of your head in the morning." Be prnnised sincerely to bear it in mind, And at dinner at first he was cautious, And though very good he the sherry did find

He sipped it ;.s-tho' it was nauseous. , But wine will the best resolution destroy. By degrees he forgot his wife's warning ; 'rho he said with each glass" now be cautious, my boy, And think of your head in the morning." in the course of the night he was asked for a toast, And he gave like a man of discerning, " The friend we can ttust with the girl we love best Who will think of your head in the morning." " Bravo " said they—" That's a capital say," And they rose up, their glasses all turning. -Mister Jennings's sentiment—hip hip—hurra, Oh, think of your head in the morning. On leaving the party, with drink nearly blind, He fell 'gainst a pump near a turning, He reel'd and he said, " Sir, that's not very kind, Consider my head in the morning." Then he roll'd in the kennel—" Sir, that's very unkind, You might, sir, have givem me warning," Then covered with Mud—as belay there he said, _ . .

How spruce I shall look in the morning. At last he got home, with his hat without brim, And he said to his wife, rather fawning, "I've been struck by a brute, because I said to him Consider your head in the morning." 'lhen too tipsy for bed, as he lay on the floor, Now he caught it for slighting the warning. "Now arn't you ashamed, sir ?"—"My dear, say no more, But think of my head in the morning." With his brain swimming round, as he lay on the ground, Only think of his head in the morning. Tho' he fell asleep sound—next day he was found Repenting, and grunting and yawning. Soda water and broth, and for moral no doubt, His spou•ie repeating her warning : "Now when you go out to your next drinking bout, Perhaps you'll think of your head in the morning."

THE MISER'S MAN. Air.—" Here we go, up-up-up." Oh, dear, these are shocking hard times, The like of 'ern never was known, Through living with old miser Grimes I'm nothing but mere skin and bone. In fact, I am wasting away, I'm getting thin as a rat, I declare. Why my wages from this miserly man, Are only four pounds in the year. Out of that I have got to find clothes, But yet this old miserly elf, I'm sure you would never suppose Is actually rolling in pelf. His temper is worse than a Turk, I do all his odd jobs,l declare, In fact I'm his maid of all work,
But I only get four pounds a year. My living it being so hard, There's no fear of my getting the gout ; I pities the rats and the mice; . ..

-For like skeletons, they all run about. Tvvas only this morning, the ninny, He swore as my nose he did handle, From my wages be would stop a penny, 'Cause I bit a piece of his candle. 'Twas but this morning again, As his hand my shoulder he pats, After looki ig awhile at his cupboard He s.nt me for a ha'porth of sprats. I fetched 'ern, I cooked 'em in grease, And what do you think ?—to my sorrow, When we'd eaten a mouthful apiece, He put the rest by till to-morrow. At night in the cellar I'm packed, Where there's only a sack for my bed, Every window is broken or cracked And I've nothing to cover my head. The rats they come gnawing my toes, Because they find oaught on the shelf, But I never drives one away—'cause I knows, What it is to be hungrApyself. Often when I pass by a cook shop, My hands in my pockets are fumbling; The smell it invites me to stop All the time that my bowels are grumbling. When I see a dog gnawing a bone, Which is given by some good-natured elf, So much do I en,vy the treat, That I steal it and gnaw it myself. I really would leave him to-morrow, That is if I my wages could get; Although they've now been due a month There's never a farthing paid yet. ' To the workhouse I'd quickly go stumping, . . _ .
Tho' a place 'tis Ido not a-driiire, - For folks say I should only be jumping, From the frying pan into there.

When we come iight down to the solid fact, the power of the press is simply steam. May be this is the reason why it gets so.many men into hot water. The sweetest flowers are those which shed their odours in quiet nooks and dingdes and the purest hearts are those whose deeds of love are done in solitude and secret.

The way to wealth is as plain as the way to market; it depends chiefly on two words—industry and frugality; that is, waste neither time nor money, but make the best lase of both. Along with the news that whalebone is scarcer, comes the information that the latest fashionable corset is bone- less. You can sometimes make a vanity as well as a virtue of 'necessity.

_ When a boy is ordered against his will to take the coal scuttle' downstairs and till it, it is astonishing the num- ber of articles he will accidentally strike that scuttle (against before getting back. Judge every man by what he cannot do and you would find no man of ability. Judge every man by what he has accomplished in. the fields with which he is familiar and you get at his real calibre. It is easy in the world to live after the world's; opinion it Is easy la militude to live after our own. But the great man is he who, in the midst of the crowd, keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude. A man was sitting for his photograph. The ;operator said DlEmr, sir.-look kind o' pleasant; smile a little." The man smiled, but the operator exclaimed:, "Oh. that will never do I It is too wide for the instrument." , _ -

THE LABOITRING MAN THREE HUN- DRED AND FIFTY YEARS AGO. Readers of "Notes and Queries" may be interested in a few facts respecting the condition of the English labourer three centuries and a half ago. In the year A.D. 1514 the rates of wages were fixed by Act of Parliament. Skilled workmen (bricklayers, carpenters, Sze.) were paid 50. a day; common labourers earned 4d. a day in the summer and 3d. in the winter. If boarded and lodged by his master the farm labourer received 16s. Bd. a year in money and 4s. in clothing. Mowers were paid Bd. a day, and harvest work was done by the piece. These wages, ; to the English labourer of modern times, will seem ridiculously low, but it must be remembered that for all the necessaries oflife a penny then went as tar as or farther than a shilling does now. The average price of wheat was 10d. a bushel. Beef and pork were a half-penuy per pound and mutton three farthings. A pig cost 4d., and a hen2d. Strong beer wase penny a gallon,and table a half-penny agallon. We have no information as to the rent of a labourer's cottage; but a law was passed in the reign of Elizabeth, enacting that no cottage should be built without four, acres of land being attached to it for the use of the cottager; and Bishop liatimer's father held a farm that employed six labourers,and fed 100 sheep and 30 cows, and for this he only paid .f. 3 or , .£4 a year. Again,every parish:then had no lands on which the poor, man might turn out his cattle, pigs; and geese free of expense. There were no Poor Laws in those days; but vagrancy was, nevertheless, a criminal ,offence. The old or infirm, who could not work, might go to a magistrate, who would give them a written license to ask for broken victuals of their richer neighbours, but no money was ever to be given to them; all money offered to be handed over to the Priest and ,Churchwardens, by whom it was to be collected every Sunday or Holy-day, and distributed to the necessitous. Able-bodied beggars were, for th,E; first offence, whipped a the curt's tail; for the second offence they lost an ear; and for the third offence the other ear was cut off. A later Act of Parliament made the third offence punishable with death. Another excellent, but severe, Act empowered the parish officers to take up all idle children above the age of five years, and "appoint them to masters of husbandry, or other craft of labour to be taught." And any child thus apprenticed, and running away without reasonable cause, was to be publicly whipped.-11. MooRE, Burnley

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 17, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 17, 1890.
" CAPITAL " CHAT.
Mr. John Dillon is to act as best man at Mr. William O'Brien's wedding. The ceremony will probably be performed by Archbishop Croke.
The latest novelty in Bond-st. art pottery is the so-called " Crumpy Ware." It looks like soft, un- baked clay, and is " crumpled " into little flower- pots, vases, and other dainty devices.

The French scnlptor Chapu has nearly finished a marble statue of the Princess of Wales, which is to be placed in the National Art Gallery at Copenhagen. The Princess is represented in a sitting position. It is to cost £10;000.

Everything connected with the proposed additions to Osborne has been left to the discretion of Princess Beatrice, which confirms the impression which has long prevailed that the queen has made her the heir of her Majesty's Isle of Wight estate.

Mr. Burt and Mr. Pickard have left for Brussels for the purpose of attending an International Con- ference of Miners in that city. Later they will be joined by their colleagues in the House of Commons —Mr. Fenwick, Mr. Crawford, and Mr. Abraham.

A number of wealthy French Jews wish to buy the Vatican copy of the Hebrew Bible from the Pope for £40,000. The Venetian Jews offered half that sum for it to Julius 11. I fancy, says a Paris correspondent, that his Holiness could not legally sell it, as he has only a life estate in the Vatican and its wealth of rare books, pictures, and fur- niture.

Mr. Benjamin Whitworth. of Manchester,ch airman of the Executive of the United Kingdom Alliance, and formerly M.P. for Drogheda, asserts that he is the oldest total abstainer in England. He is 74 years of age, and a lifelong abstainer. In 1865 the late Sir Edward Baines and Mr. Whi:worth were the 'only teetotal members of the House of Commons. Now there are upwards of 50.

The Dowager Lady de Ros, who was born in 1795, still survives, at the advanced age of ninety-five, in excellent health, nnd as keenly interested in life as ever. Lady de Ros—then Lady Georgina Lennox— was present at the celebrated ball which was given by her father, the fourth Duke of Richmond, at Brussels, the night before the Battle of Waterloo. Few other ladies now living can boast of having danced with "Wellington" that night.

The attack upon the Government, on Monday, by the member for Barrow was very damaging, and some of his points were as happy as they were effective. Mr. Goschen had described the sum pro- posed to be set apart for compensation purposes as a " nest-egg." Yes, replied Mr. Caine; but he asked, did the Chancellor ever keep poultry. If he aid, he ought to have known that the nest-egg is a sham egg put into the nest in order to induce the hens to lay real eggs.

When miners ask bra rise of wages the coal- owners loudly complain that profits are very small, but when coalowners convert their concerns into Limited Liability Companies they sing quite in a different key. Ferndale, South Wales, is being sold to a company with a capital of £775,000. The offi- cial statement of the average peofits for the last few years shows that they averaged .E 65,000 while last par they rose to £lOO,OOO. Let us keep that in mind the next time the miners are censured for asking for an additional 5 per cent.

Among our American cousins who are now on a visit to London is Major Pond, the well-known American impresario. The last time the major was here he was the agent, and the friend even more than the agent, of poor Henry Ward Beecher. It was amusing, and in some respects touching, to see the two men together. Whenever he wanted to make a joke, the great preacher always put it in some way or other on his agent. " I get Pond to write all my autographs." Or, " When people try to wake me up on a railway journey, I always let Pond personate me " ; and so on.

There is a characteristic story about Mr. James Nasmvth, showing the confidence he felt in the effectiveness of his own invention. It was on the occasion of the trial of his chef d'ecuvre. To show the gradation of the hammer's force, he placed his watch under it. Owing, however, to some mistake, the wrong power was put on,the hammer descended with a blow fit to shake a parish, and the watch was smashed into a million atoms. Nothing daunted, in order to prove the sincerity of the error, Mr. Nasmyth placed his hand under, and the hammer came down this time with the required gentle- ness.

Prince Albert Victor had an opportunity on Tues- day of publicly expressing his satisfaction with his Indian Tour. On resuming his military duties at York he was welcomed by the Corporation of that city, and his reply to the address presejited to him contained the reference to his "interesting, instrtic- tive, and pleasing tour." The Prince is reported to have added that India was a country which every Englishman who has the welfare of the Empire at heart should visit. Unfortunately it is not every Englishman with the welfare of the Empire at heart that has the opportunity for travel enjoyed by Prince Albert Victor.

The information given in a St. Petersburg paper about the possibility of the German Emperor's second son, Prince Eitel, being raised to the Imperial throne of Austria is not wholly unfounded. But the con- dition would be marriage with the Archduchess Elizabeth. She is his senior, but the difference is not great enough to be disparity when both reached years of discretion. The Queen was older than Prince Consort, and the late Comtesse de Chambord had in point of seniority by three years the advan- tage of her illustrious husband. Maria Leczineka was seven years older than Louis XV. Was not our Queen Charlotte also the senior of George 111 ? Josephine was nearly fourteen years older than Napoleon.

An interesting if not entirely new, story was told by Mr. Chamberlain in his speech at the dinner of the Artists' Benevolent Institution. It was the story of an artist who considered himself overpaid —no less a luminary of the artistic firmament than David Cox. The dealer had sold a picture by Cox for 450 guineas, and he took a pride in saying that there was a particular history connected with the work. He bought it in Cox's studio for £lO, and a few days after the bargain Cox came to him with a conscience-stricken face, and said that the price of the picture was a little too high, and he gratefully returned him £2! It was on the ground that the dealer was young, and had a wife and children. Let us hope the dealer thought a little Of David Cox and his heirs when he found a pur- chaser for the work at 450 guineas.

A story concerning an English actor‘ who was a member cif a company recently snowbound in the Sierras while en rattle from California to the East is told by the "Philadelphia Enquirer." Before their train was pulled out of the drifts they had been reduced to eating the coarse fare of the rail-v road labourers, and got little enough even of that, so that they all had a magnificent hunger on when the train reached a small station at which there was a restaurant, and the Englishman was the first to find a seat at the table. "Bring me in a hurry," he said to the landlord, a 'burly Western man," a porter-house steak, some devilled kidneys, a brace of chops, plenty of vegetables, and two bottles of Bass's bitter beer." The landlord stuck his head out of the dining-room window and yelled to somebody in the rear of the auartment ; "Say. Bill, ' tell the band to play Rule Britannia;' the Prince of Wales is in here r

Mr. Herkomer was on Tuesday elected a Royal Academician. On this occasion the General Assembly of Academicians are not likely to hear any unfavourable criticism of their appointment. Its fitness is unquestionable. It is a promotion by merit from the ranks of the Associates, leaving a vacancy there for the satisfaction of other, and, we may add, very numerous claims. In Mr. Herkomer's election no one branch of Art in unduly favoured. He is an all-round artist, who has graduated, so to speak, in many branches. In him the painters in water colours, the oil painters, the etchers, and the art professors have their representative. As the founder of the famous art school at Bushey, with its lofty ideals its theatre, and its highly artistic presentations of " Scenes in ye Olden time," he has special qualifications for aiding the educational designs of the Royal Academy. The only wonder is that/this modern master has not sooner been made an R.A. But Royal Academy distinctions do not follow with promptitude an artist's arrival at fame. It was four years after the great picture of the Chelsea Pensioner was exhibited before Mr. Herkomer was made an However, his latest distinction has found him still young. Mr, Herkomer is only 41,
MEIN'S NEW EXPEDITION.
TERRIBLE MORTALITY.

The "Times" contains a telegram from Zanzibar, which says :—The Etnin Pasha expedition, which hft Bagamoyo on the 24th ult., has only reached a distal ce of five miles from the coast, with the loss of more ti an one-fourth of the porters through death and desertion.

div.head: AN AFRICAN ROMANCE.
div.p: AN AFRICAN ROMANCE.

Poor King Dinah Salifou's visit to the Paris Exhibition was an ill-fatedone for him. That good natured African chief, says a Paris correspondent, went back to his subjects so delighted with the Exhibition and all he had seen that he wished to transform his state into a tropical France. Decree after decree was issued with this inten- tion, until at last his subjects got tired of the new mould- ing process, and conspired together and murdered him. The dusky monarch was a magnificent sr ecimen of the West African black, and the admiration of all the sculptors and painters who saw him at the Exhibition fetes at the Elys6e, where he sometimes wore a Greek dress and sometimes a bishop's vestment which he had bought in the Spanish Court of the Exhibition. The despatch telling of his assassination is silent about the fate of his wife, Queen Phillis.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO MR. T. B. POTTER.
div.p: THE PRESENTATION TO MR. T. B. POTTER.

Mr. T. B. Potter was, on Monday, presented with an address by the members of the Cobden Club in recogni- tion of his services to free trade. Mr. Gladstone, through whom the presentation was made, said that free trade having passed through periods of struggle and of triumph had now entered one of danger. He was greatly dis- appointed to see how much ground the doctrines of free trade had lost within the last twenty-five years, and for much of this the dreadful militarism which lay like an incubus upon Europe was responsible, though free trade had receded in countries where militarism did not pre- vail. Especially was this the case in the United States and some of the colonies, although he had hopes even there of the ultimate success of free trade principles. Mr. Gladstone condemned the Sugar Bounties Bill, and spoke of bimetallism as an attempt in some way to bring about a rise of prices.

div.head: MR W. O'BRIEN'S MARRIAGE.
div.p: MR W. O'BRIEN'S MARRIAGE.

By his intended marriage with Mdlle. Sophie Raffa- lovich, Mr. Wm. O'Brien, M.P., curiously enough, will become closely related to an important Russian official and to an English poet. Mdlle. Raffalovich, who is the daughter of one of the wealthiest merchants of Odessa, has two brothers—M. Arthur Raffalovich and M. Andre Raffalovich. The former, who, though a Russian by birth, has been educated in France, was some ten or twelve years ago private secretary to Count Schouvaloff, the then Russian Ambassador in London, and now represents in Paris the Russian Ministry of Commerce. He is, besides, an eminent writer on political economy, commerce, and finance, and has contributed many articles on these subjects to various French periodicals and to a leading Paris journal, of which he is the finan- cial editor. M. Andre Raffalovich is, like his brother, a Russian subject, but has chosen to make London his home. He has devoted much of his time to the study of English literature, and to such good purpose that he has written a volume of poetry denoting literary ability of no mean o der. Mademoiselle Raffalovich herself has translated a number of English works into French, especially books on political and social economy.

div.head: BANQUET TO LORD HARTINGTON.
div.p: BANQUET TO LORD HARTINGTON.

Lord Hartington was entertained on Tuesday night at the Crystal Palace at a banquet given by prominent mem- bers of the Unionist party to congratulate him on his recovery from illness, and to assure him of their confid- ence in him as a political leader. Mr. .1. Chamberlain, M.P., presided, and proposed, "Our Guest, Lord Harting- ton." Lord Hartington, in respondine, to the toast, said he was grateful for the reception theyha.d given him. He paid a high tribute to Lord Derby, Mr. Goschen, and others, who had assisted in the onslaught on the Home Rule project, and said that no member of the Unionist party could thilik that their efforts had been otherwise than successful. They had, at all events, secured that if the country ever accepted a Home Rule bill it would not be accepted without adequate consideration and discussion. Partly by their assistance and support the Government had been able to show that in Ireland Home Rule was not the only panacea, and that some approach might be made towards a period of contentment when a remedial policy could be developed. He then touched upon the position of the Opposition, and after stating that he had always looked upon the action of the Irish party as rather a matter for Executive interference than Parliamentary discussion, he proceeded to refer to the Parnell Commis- sion as indicating an alliance between the Irish Parlia- mentary party and the extreme section in America. In these circumstances he did not think that while the con- nection lasted between the Liberals and the Nationalists any desire would be aroused in him or his friends to return to the party with Which they had formerly acted. Lord Derby also spoke.

div.head: LIONISING 11R. STANLEY.
div.p: LIONISING 11R. STANLEY.

Mr. and the Baroness Burdett-Coutts entertained Mr. H. M. Stanley at dinner in Stratton-st. on Saturday evening. The Princess Louise and the Marquis of Lorne were present, and the company included the officers who accompanied Mr. Stanley through 'Africa, Lieut. Stairs. Surgeon Parke, Captain Nelson, and Mr. Mounteney Jephson ; the Emin Relief Committee (of ,which Mr. Burdett Coutts is a member), Lady Mackinn' on Lady de Winton, Lady Pelly, Mrs. Grant, Mrs. Bruce (Dr. Living- stone's daughter), the Duchess of St. Albans, the Duke and Duchess of Westminster, the Duchess of Cleveland, the Duke and Duchess of Afiercorn, Lord and Lady Wim- I borne and Hon. Miss Guest, Lord and Lady Knutsford, the Chancellor of the Exchequer and Mrs. Gosehen, Hon. Mrs. Cavendish, the Lord Advocate arid Mrs. Robertson, Lady Stewart and Miss Tombs, Sir Henry Verney, Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, M.P., Mr. and Mrs. Buckle, Dr. W. H. Russell, Miss Spencer Chapman and Miss Peel. The Baroness Burdett-Cutts afterwards held a reception ex- pressly to meet the great African traveller.

AT THE GUILDHALL. Mr. Stanley was the chief guest of the Lord Mayor of London at a conversazione in the Guildhall on Tuesday evening. In acknowledging the presentation of a casket intended to hold the record of the resolution by which the Court of Common Council conferred upon him the freedom of the city, Mr. Stanley said he honestly wished Emin every success within the limits of the German sphere of influence. Every piece of good fortune he had would rebound beneficially to England. Only downright indifference on the part of the Germans would be fatal to English enterprise, beca,use the English people were never able to show their best qualities until they were goaded to activity by rivalry. The Germans had immense odds in their favour. They had a vigorous, wide-awake monarch, and Wissmann had never heard of such things as Quakerism, peace societies,anti-enterprise companies, and namby-pamby journalism—the clogs of every hearty endeavour in this country.

div.head: MEMBER FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE MEMBER FOR WARRINGTON.

The "Star' _says :—"'Sir Gilbert Greene/1, M.P. for Warrington: and lord of the Wilderspool Brew- ery, with its mine hundred houses closely "tied," is probably worth a couple of millions or more, and is not, unnaturally, of paramount local influence. , In- deed, his influence (inherited and increased) in a Radical town of Irish elements, early secured the triumph of the Conservative party at the elections —a service which Lord Beaconsfield acknowledged and perpetuated by the gift of a baronetcy. Sir I Gilbert, who—now over eighty—mostly performs his Parliamentary dutieiby pairing, passes his time between his busy breweries and the unostentatious comfort of Walton IJall. kfere, within sight of the sumptuous church his beeflaas built, but unable to see the limit of his distant fields and farms, he spends a quiet ,country life with his wife (the most vigorous of nurses) and his two daughters. If heis troubled by any feeling of regret, it is perhaps that his only son prefers horses and'hunting to brewing I beer and catch lag voters." SIR GlLDiit'S BIRTHDAY. • -

On Sunday Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., member of Parliament for the borough of Warrington, attained his 84th birthday, he having been born at Wilders- pool on May 11, 1806. In celebration of the event, the flag at the Conservative Club was displayed on Monday, and Sir Gilbert ' received numerous tele- grams and letters of congratulation. In point of age he is only exceeded by three other members of the House of Commons, namely, Mr. C. P. Villiers, Colonel O'Gorman Mahon, and Mr. David Pugh. Of another octogenarian M.P. it may be mentioned that Mr. Isaac Holden, who represents the Keighley division of the West Riding of Yorkshire, has just completed his 83rd year, he having been born on I May 7, 1807.

div.head: CHAPTER EXT. vim CLOCK TOO FAST.
div.p: CHAPTER EXT. vim CLOCK TOO FAST.

Total was another pleasant tea prepared at Ladyship. terrace, for, by note this time, Mr. Alfred Denville had sent word that he was coming. There was joy in Ladyship-terrace at the announce- ment, in the hearte of both mistress and maid, and when the visitor arrived in evening dress, Lizzy- beth Ann declared that he was the handsomest gentle- man she ever see, while Mrs. Appleby's eyes looked her admiration in a most unmistakeable way. The little lady was so happy in her choice, and her mature heart had budded out so green and fresh, that she looked quite young again, and more than once she blushed when she caught herself looking in the glass to see if she would look much too old beside her young' swain. Glasses always were deceptive, and this one, large and old as it was, proved to be no better than the rest; for it grossly flattered the little widow, who fell into such a state of fluttered gratification that she made endless mistakes over the tea, and was constantly ex- cusing herself to her guest. So happy and satisfied was the little lady that she failed to notice how many times her maid came into the room. She certainly noticed that Lizzybeth gazed a great deal at Mr. Denville; but she was not at all surprised at this, for Alfred was so handsome that it was only natural. She had never seen him before to such advantage, for he had confided to her that—thanks to the money she had lent him—the solicitor had said that he fel: perfectly sure new of bringing the opposite party to their knees, and, consequently, his mother's aiTain Would be comfortably settled, and he should have Lis own. This good news had had a wonderful effect upon his spirits, and he laughed and chatted, mid flattered the little body in the most astonishing way, and to her great delight. Perfectly sincere and guileless herself, she felt no doubt of her lover's words. It was evident that he loved her very much, and that evening seemed to pass like magic. She was rather uncomfortable in her mind upon one point though, and that was the supper. "Dear Alfred" had announced thbt he must go away by ten o'clock, and Lizzybeth was not always to be trusted as to punctuality. The consequence was that, twice over, little Mrs. Appleby had to leave the room, and on the second occasion she had not returned many minutes before, glancing at the timepiece upon the mantel boz.rd, she uttered a loud exclamation. "Oh, look at the time:" she said. "That clock must be fast. Why, it's three quarters of an hour before my watch. It can't be so late as that." Her visitor looked at his own watch, smiled, and turned the face towards her. "Only four minutes met," he said. "But you must be fast, too," she exclaimed. "Let me look at the clock in the passage." She trotted out to come back wide-eyed. "You are quite right, Alfred, dear,' she exclaimed. "That clock is just the same. I couldn't have believed it was so late." " Time flies so fast when I am bare," he said, with a languishing look; and the poor little lady blushed and sighed, and said it did. And as she said that, she thought how nice it would be if, instead of having to live alone any longer. Alfred were to come and keep her company. It could be so easily managed she thought, as she re-arranged his tie: the house was already fur- nished, and there was plenty of room for one more. She was not a young, weak girl now, who did not know her own mind; and what would be easier than for them to go out together quietly some day, walk into a church without any fuss, and walk out again with nobody but themselves the wiser? If she were only a man, how soon it would have been settled; but as it happened she was only a woman, and of course she must wait until Alfred proposed such a step himself. Once as they sat down to supper, she thought that he had some such intentions, but no: he was all vivacity, delightful company, and drank her health several times with the prettiest of speeches. She sighed and he sighed when ten o'clock arrived, for they had had to hurry over the supper. " But must you go—so soon?" she said. She spoke so imploringly that he told her, in what she felt to be quite touching language, that everything must give way to her, and resuming his seat be stayed till the little timepiece over the tire chimed for eleven. when he tore himself away.
CHAPTER XXIL MR. RLOPSTOCIL IN BED.

OLD Mr. Klopstock had several bad habits. Old bachelors generally have. Moral for gentlemen: Don't be an old bachelor, if you wish to lead a blameless life. The old manager's habit of taking snuff has already been mentioned, and perhaps be might have left that off, but his sister referred to it so frequently that out of obstinacy he kept it on. Nothing, however, has been said about his habit of reading in bed, as bad a bachelor habit as can exist. He used to say that unless be read in bed he would never have gone to sleep, and hence it was a necessity. This was the old manager's idea, and probably he liked his book or paper of a night, or else he would have considered that men are creatures of custom, and that they can soon diet themselves to almost any manner of living. But that was the fact. The old gentleman thoroughly enjoyed setting his shaded lamp beside the bed, giving the pillow a few good punches to get it into a satis- factory shape, full of support for his back, adjusting his nightcap so that the tassel hung over his nose, putting on his spectacles, doubling his paper to a handy size, and then settling down for a good, long

read. It never really troubled the old gentleman that he was as good as alone in the great place, for the maids were in the attic, and the under-porter in the basement; nor after getting himself snug in bed, did he ever pause to think of the large amounts in cash and securities, and often in jewels, that would be safely locked up in Mr. Middlecombe's patent vault, the keys of whose juggle- tumbler locks were in his possession. " I'm not going to fidget and make myself miserable about the money.' he had said many a timo at the Woolfords'. "Some people rush off to banks with it, where it isn't half so safe. We don't, only when it suits us; and if we do run risks, so do people who put their money in banks. There it is, locked up as fast as can be, and I've got the keys. What's the use of a strong vault if you don't use it?" "No," he would say, " I shan't make my life miser- able. The place is well watched by the police, and as to myself, if I sat up and watched one night, I couhtn't do it another, for a man must have sleep; and even if I could watch for two nights, the burglars, if thy came, would be sure to come upon the third, so what good should I do? No; there are the pistols, and I've •got the blunderbuss, and I must take my chance. Places of business are not robbed every day." So when in health he used quietly to see that all was fast, and go to bed exactly at eleven o'clock, Ed- wards, the under-porter, doing likewise; but upon thic one particular night it was Samson Hall who °ems pied the under-porter's room. That was a strange shadow cast upon the wall of the large room as the old man half reclined in heel reading. It was a large, shadowy room—one that had been a withdrawing room in its day, and so strange shadows were not out of place. As he read on and on, the tassel of his night-cap vibrated, and the grotesque outline seemed to dance up and down in a weird fashion that had something roblin-like in its aspect, as it trembled on the dim. grey wall. Now the figure moved a little one way, now another, and then it seemed to be fading away as the lamp grew dim, but a touch from the old man's hand, and the goblin-like shadow came out well defined „once more. The matter which the old man read was very interesting, and he grunted approval at times, though at other times he uttered an impatient " pish!" when the shadow of the night-cap with its tassel gave a sharper jerk than usual. Then, as he read on, the paper would slowly descend towards the counterpane, and lie there till, with quite a start, the old gentleman would rouse up, cough to clear his throat, readjust the paper, and go on reading )nee more. This had happened several times as per custom (as :ommercial men whuld say), when it became evident .:hat the reading was pretty well over for the night. After the last slow re-arranging of the paper, and oef ore a dozen lines could have been perused, it sank softly once more upon the counterpane, the rigid hands were relaxing, and the old man sank lower and lower upon his pillow; a gasping snore began to be ' heard, and as, in place of the goblin-like shadow upon the wall, that was only now the semblance of a softly heaving heap, it was evident that poor old Klopstock was fast asleep, and that the reading lamp would have to burn itself out, according to the custom of many years.

• Five minutes passed; ten minutes; a quarter of an !our; and the big old-fashioned gold watch, with its arabic figures ticked viciously away where it was hung to the back of a washstand, giving itself such an impetus that it swung gently to and fro, as if it was disap- pointed at not having been made a clock, and was now in training to become a pendulum. All was very still, for the eastern end of the City is not a lively place by night, and what distant noises thine were, came very faintly through the double windows of the old room, where, saving the heavy breathing of the old man, all seemed still, even to oppression, and the post of watcher, supposing there to have been one by the sick bed, would have been one to try the strongest nerves. The manager's great, dull bedroom was heavily furnished in a very old-fashioned style. Everything was very good and solid, but cheerless of aspect, and in the worst of taste, for the upholsterers employed some lifty years before to furnish this room were evidently impressed with the idea that a bed-chamber in a business establishment should be always suggestive to its occupant of the counting-house below. Hence there was plenty of dark-hued mahogany, in the shape of great wardrobes and drawers, ample enough for the costumes of a fashionable dame, and never used by old Klopstock, who kept his modest two suits of clothes in a bottom drawer, and his linen in the right hand top. There were great leather-seated chairs, a sofa, a couple of lounges, and the large, massive-loolixig, four- post bedstead, with a great canopy at the top, and an abundance of hangings and fringes, giving it the ale pearance of a funeral car used at some state inter meet.

Such a room required plenty of light to make it bearable, but with only Mr. lilopstoci'enreadine lamp to illumine it, the place seemed to be always full of lurking shadows in dark corners that kept creeping forward, as if to spring upon him when the lights:uric, but shrank back when it was trimmed. Quite half an hour had passed, and the old man's heavy breathing 'told that he was sleeping soundly. The shaded lamp still burned, and now cast its light upon the puckered countenance of the sleeper, that looked worn and haggard with his late ailment. Darkness here and darkness there, while, facing the bed, the glow from the lamp seemed to be reflected from the polished surface of a chest of drasers, the tall wardrobe in the futher corner merely looming out

_ of the intense gloom. Suddenly there was a sharp crack as if another of he flints of the weapons over the mantelpiece bad fallen, or it might have been the weather affecting the woodwork of one of the great pieces of furniture, well

seasoned as it was. - But the noise had not penetrated old Klopstock's sleep-deadened ears; his breath came regularly as before, and his old features looked as grotesque as ever, 'ying full in the glow of the lamp. Creak! Creak! Crack! Then silence, and the greater part of the room ir darkness; but, in the thickest of the gloom, one of the doors of the great wardrobe had swung open to its

fullest extent. Once mere there was the regular breathing of the old man; then a soft rustling noise, and one of the black shadows of the room seemed to come forward on to the thick, soft carpet, ancl stand there silent and watchful in the gloom. Fast asleep. and breathing regularly, for the old manager had had several wakeful, feverish nights, and this was a general making up for what he had lost. Sleeping peacefully without any painful dream to make him start awake; no warning of impending danger, for the dark shadow were an ominous look, as it stood there without movement for some minutes. Was it a shadow, or was it substance? Strange patches of darkness came and went so in that great room that for a time one lying in that bed might have been in doubt. But shadows come and go in silence, and there was faint rustling here, repeated as the dark appearance seemed to bend down, and go upon hands and kneec. creeping softly along towards the side of the bed. tc which the old man had his back half turned. There was a minute's pause of busy preparation, and than the figure rose, showing, in the soft light of a lamp, a heavily-bearded man, apparently or stout build, whose cheeks and forehead were darkened by a band of crape—ominoue suggestion of mourning for some one daad. In the dim light he seemed to be dressed in a dart closely-fitting jersey and sailor's loose trousers, while a light skull cap with the ear-protectors tiol down by the strings beneath his chin served the double purpose of protection and holding on the crape mask. As he stood there listening, and with his watchful eyes glitering, his whole get up was that of a burglar of the accepted type, and he held something dark in his left hand, a short thick staff like that of a constable in the other. There was the distant rattle of a cab, and a gust of wind wandering amidst the City lanes rattled the outer window. The old man moved uneasily, and the dark watcher glided behind the hangings. But the long-drawn breathing told that the old manager was sleeping soundly, and, gliding back to his former position, the midnight visitor stood listening for a few moments, and then softly placing his left knee upon the bed, he leaned over and placed what now showed in the light of the lamp as a sponge, upon old Klopstock's half-open mouth and nose. Rousing up in alarm at the touch, the old man wrenched his face away, gazed up in his assailant's face and uttered a hoarse cry; but as it was leaving his lips, the staff fell heavily twice upon his forehead, and his head dropped back upon his pillow. The next instant the sponge was once more pressed heavily on his mouth and nostrils, the old man's feeble struggles ceased, and he lay passive there with the sponge kept in its place by a pillow being dragged forward, and laid against his cheek. "Old fool!" said the assailant, hoarsely; and, going to the mantel pzece, he struck a match, lit a little dark lantern, and, evidently quite at home, took a key trout the pocket of the old man's trousers. With this key he opened a drawer in the dressing- table, wherein lay a bunch of glittering keys, and after securing these, he walked quickly back to the bedside, took a bottle from his pocket, removed the cork, and poured its contents upon the sponge. "Make him sleep," he muttered, as he threw the bottle on the bed, glanced round, held the staff re fly, and, stepping lightly back in his golosh-covered feet, he took a leather bag from the great wardrobe, unlocked the chamber Jeer, stood listening, withdrew the key, and inserted it on the other side, ended by locking the old man in, and then paused on the landing. All was perfectly still, and rapidly descending the broad staircase, as if quite at home in the place, he opened the door leading into the counting-house with a large old key, and once more stood listening as he closed the lantern, and stuck it in the waistband of his trousers. Next, going down on hands and knees, he gathered himself as it were for a spring, and made one that was quite cat-like, landing him behind one of the partitions which screened him from the view of any inquisitive policeman who might have been peering through the blind from the narrow lane. Every act showed that he was familiar with the place; that his movements were all in accordance with carefully thought-out plans, and that be was full, aware of the building being kept lit up for the sake of the security. It had not occurred to Mr. Klopstock and the prin- cipals, though, that after bounding across that narrow passage, an ingenious man could keep himself under cover'until he reached the manager's room, and that by remaining upon his hands anti knees, he was quite below the glass partitioning, and consequently as safe— perhaps more so—from the absence of suspicion as if he were in the dark. "Now for the fire and burglar-proof vault," said the nocturnal visitor, drawing aside a brass slide, in serting a key, and throwing open the door leading down into the vault; and quickly descending, he turned on his bull's eye, went straight to a ledge where there were matches, and turned on and lit a jet of gas. Having done this, he hesitated, and ran back to the steps to satisfy himself as to whether there would be an additional glare of light ascending into the manager's room. It made no difference, and hurrying back, he applied key after key, and as easily as the groat rock gateway of Aladdin's cave, the various ebstaeles were put back, till the last mwsive door had glided aside, and he stood gazing into the inner safe, where Martin Woolford had passed so many hours. Here he turned on another gas jet, lit it, and -nesitated for a moment to think. No, he would not want the lantern again, and it was an encumbrance, so, opening and blowing it out, he threw it in a corner, and having used the last of Mr. Middlecombe's bright keys, he had before him the objects of his search in one of the smaller cupboard- like safes. Here, ranged before him, were a number of canvas' bags—some large, some small, and of these he selected six, each with a label attached, bearing the magic figures 500, and representing in all three thousand pounds in sovereigns. These he deposited in the leather travelling hag, noised it by the handles for a few moments, and

hesitated. • "Shall I take more?" he muttered, gazing with gloating eyes upon quite a drzm more Rich bags. "No; won't do. Ther,'s a long way to go, and half a hundred-weight to carry now." But though he would not allow himself to be

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: tempted into taking more gold, there was other treasure there; and, turning to a steel drawer, he took out a note case, slit it open with a penknife, uttered an im- patient " pish !" and threw it aside. Several more locked cases shared this fate. Then he opened one, uttered an ejaculation indicative of satisfaction, as he saw that it was well filled with bank notes; found another, which, on being cut open, was equally satisfactory ; and then from another drawer took one bulky pocket-book, which he did not slit, but placed at once with the other books in the black bag, literally wrenched himself away from the spoil before him, and closed and locked his black bag, bending down on one knee, and fastening the straps with clever fingers that looked very white. "Quite heavy enough," he said, as the temptation was on him to take more. "This will do, so now for safety." He quickly closed the principal drawers, and was in ' the act of stooping to pick up his bag, when he fancied that he heard a step. For a moment his heart stood still ; then, picking up the bag with one hand, he extinguished the little jet of gas, and felt for the short heavy staff. Gone! He bad laid it down somewhere ready to hand, and be could not tell where. He muttered a curse at his folly, but there was not a moment to lose. The step he had heard was, perhaps, only fancy, but the manager might recover at any time, and go to his window and shout for help. It was time he was off, so with the heavy bag in his hand, he made for the passage, but there was no mis- take this time: there was a step, and drawing aside, he waited, for his retreat was out off. Oh, for that staff—a pistola knife—anything; but he was unarmed, and hese, with a heavy kitchen poker in his hand, was Sams& Hall, coming cautiously along the narrow vault passage with outstretched neck. peering about for the meaning of the open door. In an instant he ought sight of the dark figure standing there, and fell back stunned, uttering a groan, for, with tremendous force, the heavy leather - bag was dashed in his face, driving his head against the steel walls of the vault, and then he fell with a thud, his head striking tho steel floor with suflicient force to stun him, if the other blow had not already had the result. The burglar snatched up the poker, which Jell clanging down, and prepared for the next assailant., but all was still, the attack having been so sudden that the unfortunate man had had no opportunity for raising an alarm, and standing the poker aside, the man carried his bag to the stairs, stepping over the prostrate body ; then returning, he leaped over it again, seized it by the legs, dragged it in right through to the farthest part of the strong room, and with deft hands closed door and grating. "Let him shout now," muttered the burglar. "Meddling fool!" and he paused for a moment to All still, and he ascended, closed and locked th 6 door at the top of the steps, thrust his hand up the chimney, and dropped the keys behind• the regi4Br- stove, and then sat there panting. "How came he here ?" he muttered. "Well, it hi tomes to he may shout until he is hoarse. My word, it's warm work. Must have something to drink, if r to fps it, sod—Hallo! What'a that?" as fro socatinusel.)

A German contemporary has the following story upper Heiduk, in Silesia, a working-man sold his wife f° a term of two years to an acquaintance for a shilling. ; The wife lived with her new partner in harmony, whtll one day the lawful husband thinking he had surrander her too cheaply, called, upon the man and demandeq further sum of fifteen shillings. The lady, he said, ha a set of beautiful teeth. He had forgotten that, and 0' considered fifteen shilling a small sum under the circeo2" stances. "The man in possession" demurred. and Or,. husband sought the aid of the law. The authorities, appears, pronounced that as he had contracted himse" .out of his legal rights for two years, and for a shilling* he was not entitled to any further amount.
