HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNnes. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at a quarter-past four. THE NEW ConE.—Lord NORTON called attention to the new Education Code, and said it was an improvement on that introduced last year and withdrawn. The two together were a considerable improvement on the exist- ing law.—Lord CRAM:11100X was pleased to find that no serious objection had been taken to the new code, in the framing of which her Majesty's inspectors had been largely consulted. The result wa-s,that so lone as schools Were efficient they wculd get a fixed grant, but schools Which were not efficient would disappear altogether.— The subject eventually dropped. Bitcs AnyeEcEn.—The Open Spaces Bill and the Com- missioners .for Oaths Act (1889) Amendment Bill passed through Committee. The House adjourned at half-past six. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE VOLUNTEERS.—MT. STANHOPE informed Sir H. Havelock Allan that he proposed to issue to all volun- teers outside the metropolitan district either the neces- larY equipment or its estimated value, 1.25. per man. In the case of artillery volunteers the sum would be ss. per roan. The Government were prepared to bear the initial cost of all equipments other than clothing for any new corps that might be formed. Thus it was hoped to solve the equipment question once and tor all. COUNTY COUNCIL FuNps.—Mr. RITCHIE, answering Mr. S. Evans, said the funds which stood to the 'credit of a county the council of which refused to expend them in faYing compensation for the extinction of public-house licenses under the Local Taxation Bill would remain at the credit, of the county at accumulated interest until Parliament had decided how they might otherwise be applied. M. GoscEEN Aim Ma. Dumme.—Mr. Goschen was questioned by Mr. Dillon as to the authenticity of the, report of his Rawtenstall speech, in which he referred to Mr. Dillon is denouncing certain proposals because they bad not emanated from the Nationalist party. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said the report Nvas a fairly accurate one. Mr. DILLON then submitted that the statement was absolutely untrue. Mr. GOSCHEN, however, repeated that he had given an accurate version of the remarks. COMPENSATION TO PUBLICANS.

- ------. Mt. Rrrcin,E moved the second reading of the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise Duties) Bill. He said the amount of money which was expected to be received by local authorities last year was considerably dimin- ished by the failure to pass the wheel and van tax, and that if the opposition of the hon. member for Barrow Was successful the Bill as a whole would have to go. Ent the Government considered their case so good that they would resist all onslaughts upon their licensing ProPosals. He maintained that Mr. • Gladstone himself and other leaders of the Liberal party had laid down that licensed victuallers had the same right to compensation aS anyone else carrying on a lawful trade. He asked the Rouse and the country to believe that their sole object was to help temperance reformers and promote the cause • temnerance. Mr. CAINE moved as an amendment" That this House declines to assent to a Bill which provides, by payment out of public moneys, for the extinction of annual loillses in the manner provided in this Bill." He said the temperance party believed the measure would seri- °usly injure the cause of temperance, and they intended tO oppose the Bill to the utmost of their power. The Liverpool Diocesan Church of England Temperance Society had passed resolutions strongly disapproving of the Government proposal, and if he could turn the Government out of office by his amendment he would do ao with pleasure. If the Bill with these clauses in it became law he should immediately start an agitation for its repeal. Mr. STOREY seconded the amendment. •Mr. T. W. Russell, Sir George Trevelyan, and others loined in the debate, which was adjourned. The House adjourned at 12.40, HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at half-past five. HISTORICAL MANUSCRIPTS COMMISSION.Ord Beau- champ moved that there be laid before this House a complete list, with dates of issue, of the reports of the Historical Manuscripts Commission.—Lord DE RAMEY, en behalf of the Home Office, said there would be no Objection to give, a return in the following form :—A complete list, dates of issue of the reports, an alphabeti- cal index of the collections examined, and an alphabeti- cal index of the owners of such collections.—The motion Was then agreed to. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly after two o'clock. THE SUGAR CONVENTION.—Sir 1. FERGUSON said the Government were not aware that Germany had been in- formed that this country intended to defer carrying out the Sugar Convention. NEW MEMBER.—Sir Joseph Weston took his seat, amid Cheers, for East Bristol. THE COMPENSATION PROPOSALS.

Sir W. HOULDSWORTH resumed the debate on the second reading of the Local Taxation (Customs and Ex- cise) Bill, and dealing with Mr. Caine's contention re- carding the support given to the Bill by the Church of -P-algland Temperance Society, said it was true this sup- Port had been given by the legislative sub-committee, but the Executive Committee, which was the central 'rgan of the society, had come to the conclusion that they would relegate the whole question to the legislative elito•committee to represent the society in regard to the Provisions of the Bill. That was how the legislative The promised support to the Government. ine Church of England Temperance Society refused to !ecognise any legal claim for compensation, assuming that the magistrates had absolute discretion, but they held that there was a very strong moral and equitable claim to a moderate, reasonable, and terminable com- Pensation. Mr. HENEAGE strongly supported the Bill for what was good in it, though he should move some amend- ments in Co nmittee. Mr. RATIIIIONE opposed the Bill on the ground that it Would add vastly to the value of licensed houses at a time when the enormous value of these houses was one of the main difficulties with which the temperance cause had to cc ntend. Mr. WALTER LONG pointed out that the proposal was lint to grant absolute compensation to publicans for the removal of their licenses. The Government merelY pro- Posed to confer upon County Councils the power to enter Into tha market as purchasers of these commodities, and y them with money provided for the purpose, and the Government believed this course would largely assist the cause of temperance. On the motion of Sir WILFRID LAWSON, the debate was adjourned. A, COUNT OUT.—On resuming, at 9 o'clock it was found there were not 40 members present, and the House was counted out. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock, but the House was not made until twenty-five Minutes past. ASCENSION DAY.—Mr. W. H. SMITH moved that, 10-

inorrow being Ascension Day, committees of the Reuse • theuld not meet before two o'clock. The motion was agreed to without a division. AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS (IRELAND) BILL. ' A GOVERNMENT DEFEAT. Dr. Fox moved the second reading of the Agricultural Labourers (Ireland) Bill, which provides for the expendi- ture of a million and a half of money out of the Irish Church surplus in the erection of cottages for agricul- tural labourers.—Mr. JOHN O'Coxxon seconded, and Mr. Jormsrox moved an amendment, based partly on the fact that the Land Purcha.se Bill provides special facilities for improving the dwellings of labourers.—Mr. T. W. RnsseLL moved the adjournment of the debate on the Eound that no explanation of the bill had been given. The motion for adjournment was rejected by a majority of 26, and the Speaker declined to act on a motion of Mr. , Parnell that the question be now put.—Mr. SMITH-BARRY trod Colonel SAUNDERSON spoke in opposition to the bill.— Air. BALFOUR said the bill was not in the main a labourers relief bill, and was a far more illiberal scheme than that in the Land Purchase Bill, and the Government would •Vaell no significance Whatever to the decision come to. The bill was then read a second time Without a division. MISCELLANEOUS.—The 'second reading of the Jury Law (Ireland) Pill, which was moved by Mr. KILBIIME, was negatived by a majority of 53. Leave was given to intro- duce several bills, which were read a first time, among them being one by Colonel Sandys,to substitute depriva- tion for imprisonment for contumacy in proceedings .Mider the Church Discipline Act of 1840 and the Public Worship Act of 1874. HOUSE OF COMMONS. T --HURSDAY.The • Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Sunday •-ioesriows &c.—Mr. J. C. _STEVENSON withdrew his Closing Bill, being of opinion that there was no 1 ),_rosnect of his'h,ing able this session to take the sense of Rouse on the measure. Sir James Ferguson informed 't Stanleyr• Bryce that the engagements entered into by Mr. with native chiefs in the interior of Africa were not made under any authority from Her Majesty's Govern- 'Lent 'Tar COMPE:ISATION BILL.—SECOND READING CARRIED. virThe debate on the Licensing Bill was resumed by Sir iLmun LAWSON, who said the bill was neither more nor cnor less than blackmail levied on the people of this ?Untry toile put into the pockets of political supporters ,21tethe Government. Mr. MATTHEWS dealt with some of ...criticisms which the Government proposals had met 'KM Mr. GIADSTOVE qaid this was a bill for the endow- ment of .a_ta nthe v with public money, and, glancing various contingencies subject to which the publi- ,c,o9.tit carried on his trade, he asserted that nothing that possi- bility happen under the existing law could by any form a just ground for endowing him with public _n tutilo ey in the event of the non-renewal of his licence -t„,mngil purchase. The compensation proposed was dangerous without ground in principle, was most -donferoos, and was totally unsupported by prece- lateaand the scheme of the Government was to throw back the temperance cause, for an inde- 'mte Period. Mr. JACOB BRIGHT, in opposing the bill, '39ld they heard O. good deal about the poor publicans,

but how much, he asked, of the purchase money of the public-houses would go to the publicans, and how much to the brewers and the limited liability companies? Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said the real serious danger of the bill was that all the purchases and the sums given would be the measure of the future compensation. In his opini- en the bill was introduced not because magistrates had not done their duty, but because they had done it, and because the liquor interests were finding that the public-houses were being put an end to without compen- sation. Mt. SMITH• having replied, the House divided, with the following result :—For Mr. Caine's amendment, 266; against, 339. The second reading of the bill was then agreed to.

div.head: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT
div.p: THE FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT
WARRINGTON.
ADJOURNED INQUEST AND VERDICT.

The adjourned inquiry as to the death of George Jones (63), a tallow chandler, who had been in the employ of Alderman Burgess, and who died from injuries received in falling down some steps at his place of employment on Friar's-green, was held on Tuesday, at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-st., by Mr. Brighouse, coroner. There were present Alder- man Burgess. Mr. Ridgway, solicitor (who repre- sented Alderman Burgess), Dr. Cannel], Dr. J. T. Smith (house surgeon at the Infirmary), Mr. E. E. Bowden (junior house surgeon), and Mr. A. Jones (son of the deceased). The Coroner mentioned that the inquiry had been ad- journed in order that a post-mortem examination of the body of the deceased might be made. That had been made by Drs. Cannell and Smith, and they would hear the result. He (the Coroner) had been at the premises where the accident occurred, and seen what it was necessary to see. Dr. Cannell, then gave evidence as to the post- mortem. He said that the body of the deceased was well nourished. There were two abrasions, a small one on the forehead, and a small abrasion on top of the scalp; the left eye was blackened; there was a slight bruise on the back as well as a slight abrasion of skin of back. There was no fracture of the skull, but the brain was somewhat congested. The eighth rib on the left side was fractured just anterior to ha angle but did not per- forate the pleura. The heart wa fatty, flabby, and dil- ated and the kidneys congested, but otherwise healthy. The cause of death was shock acting on a diseased and fatty heart. The Coroner: A question arose at the first sitting as to what ought to have been done with the deceased when presented to the officials at the Infirmary. Now that you have made a post-mortem examination can you say that those injuries were sufficiently developed to enable Dr. Smith to find them out when presented? _ _

Dr. Camell ; I do not think so. The Coroner; I mean as to this fractured rib—do you think that would be found out by examination? Dr. Cannell : Not in the condition'the man was in at the time. No doubt he was very badly shaken. He would complain of pain everywhere, and if we do not get a special sympton of pain we ddnot look for a particu- lar injury. I should not have found this fractured rib myself had I not been trying to turn the man ovee. The Coroner: Considering all the circumstances, and considering the condition of the man, do you think it was the right or wrong thing to do to send him home? Dr. Cannel!: I should certainly have sent him home if I had been in the same position as Dr. Smith. Dr. Cannell added that the reason why he should have done so was that he should not have considered that the man was sufficiently injured to be admitted to the Infirmary. He should have looked upon it as a case for simple treat- ment at home. The Foreman of the Jury (Mr. E. Pickavance) said a simpler case went to the Infirmary this week and was admitted. The Coroner said the jury would have to decided upon the particular case on the evidence and must not let local rumour and gossip come into consideration. He did not want to screen the Infirmary officials, but on the other hand he did not want them to be blamed wrongly. To Dr. Cannel!: You would most probably have acted as Dr. Smith did? Dr. Cannel!: I should most certainly have acted in the same way. The Foreman,: Dr. Cannell tells us that he found the fractured rib when he turned the man over. Could not the same thing have been done by the doctors at the Infirmary? Dr. Cannel!: Yes, but mine was simply a casual turn over; I was simply pulling the man over. I should certainly not have found the rib without specially looking for it. The Foreman: It is just what I anticipated—the man was not specially looked at. Dr. Smith, house surgeon at the Infirmary, next gave evidence. He said he was present at the post-mortem and he agreed with the evidence of Dr. Cannell on that point. The man was admitted to the Infirmary on the morning of Saturday the 3rd inst., and he (witness) had him stripped and examined as catetully as he could He complained of pains all over the back and especially on the right shoulder. Witness looked for fractured ribs because it was a thing a man having an accident like that was liable to, but he did not find any. The injured man was generally bruised and shaken, but beyond that witness found no serious injury at all. They never in any case kept in a case at the Infirmary where the injuries were so slight,and, further, he kwitness) believed the deceased was in no special danger in being moved as he had a cab and lived close by, and also that he could afford to pay for his own medical man. Seeing, therefore, that the injuries were not serious and that the patient could afford to pay for his own medical man he (witness) would not have been doing his duty to the Infirmary if he had kept, the man there. As to whether the man ' was chunk witness would state positively that he was not drunk. It had been suggested by the policeman that he (witness) turned the man out because he thought he was drunk, but that statement was absurd. He should say that at least a third of the cases brought to the Infirmary were drunk, and he kept them if he thought there was sufficient reason for it, but it was a small Infirmary and he had to make a selection By the Coroner: How was i t that this eighth rib on the left side escaped your notice ?—I suppose it must have been owing to the position I examined the man in. I had him sitting on a couch.—ls it trite possible with a careful examination to overlook a fractured rib ?—Yes it is frequently done. Besides if I had found it I should na't have aclmittedshim, as a fractured rib in itself is not a serious injury.,--This man was not denied admission because he was drunk P—On the contrary, he was not drunk.—This man received the same examination that other patients receive before admittance ?—Yes.—And the reason he was sent to his home was that it was close by, that he was able to pay to be looked after; and that you did not think he was suffering sericusly P—The last is the chief point. If I had thought he was suffering severely, no matter in what position he was, I should have kept him. I did not think he was seriously injured and the post-mortem bears that out. In answer to the Coroner, Dr. Cannell said he was not called in till Monday. He received a message a. few minutes before 10 o'clock and he called on his ordinary round. The message did not say that this was a case of life and death, and the relatives of the deceased did not convey to him the impression that they thought it was serions'case when he got there. He aid not think the man would- have died so soon. His pulse was exceed- ingly feeble. The heart seemed to fail, and to place him- self in a guarded position he' naturally said that the matter was serious; at the same time he did not think the man would have died so soon. Mr. Alfred Jones said Dr. Cannell saw his (the speaker's) brother, John, on the Monday before the death of the deceased, and remarked, " Wire to your brother at once, as the man is dangerously ill." Witness received a telegram asking him to come to Warrington, and he did so. Dr. Cannel! replied that he did not know witness had a brother. Mr. Alfred Jones said that when he saw Dr. Cannel! last Wednesday the latter said there had been perfect neglect at the Infirmary by Dr. Smith, and that he intended " to see that matter thoroughly through." Dr. Cannell : I deny it in tote. The Coroner, to Mr. Jones : Do you say that Dr. Cannel! said that to you? Mr. .Tones: He said it in his own surgery. Mr. Wm Burgess, who was called by Mr. Ridgway, said he was a grocer's assistant, and worked for his father, Mr. John Burgess. On Friday last, about ten o'clock, he went to the works on Friar's-green to maim a search,. He went into the cellar and found the trap door in the centre propped against a post. He noticed, that 'the door was spla.shed with tallow, and he formed the opinion that it had been there some time, and had been used for other purposes. Since then he had had the door put back in its place. 4 In answer to the Coroners witness said he could not say when he last saw the trap door in its place, He could Safely say that about ten years ago the trap door was in its pace. He had been away some time but since he came back four years ago he did not remember seeing the trap doer at the entrance to the cellar. The Coroner: Everything shows that the door has not been there for some length of time.

Wit less: That is so. The Coroner: And the door is not a very grand door when in its place. Witness : It answers its purpose. The Coroner: Just, but it was not there you see—that is the worst of it. The Foreman : It seems strange he should remember it ten years ago and then no: look for it four years ago. Mr. Ridgway said he wished to point out that what Alderman Burgess said about deceased being drunk at nine o'clock did not clash with what Dr. Smith said of his not being drunk at one o'clock. The Coroner, in summing up, said the deceased had worked for Mr. Burgess for a long time,and there was no doubt he was well acquainted with the premises. He (the Coroner) could not agree with the dictum of Mr. Burgess, that it was the duty of the deceased to point out defects to his employer, cr what was dangerous to life. Such an assertion was all very pretty on paper, and in theory, but a workman knew that if he lost his employment he might be unable to find work elsewhere; they were un- able to find a man who would complain about defects in the premises where he worked. He knew very well that

div.head: TB E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 17, 1890. WALKS ON THE SHIP CANAL. FROM WARRINGTON TO WARBURTON.
div.p: TB E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 17, 1890. WALKS ON THE SHIP CANAL. FROM WARRINGTON TO WARBURTON.

it amonnted to this—the employer might say," If you don't like it you must go somewhere else ' • I do not like you growling at me." If there were any defects it was the duty of Mr. Burgess not only to find them out, but to remedy them. It was beyond dispute that the deceased had to go to the first floor by a set of steps. He (the Coroner) did not think the steps were quite as bad as they had been represented to be by the evidence. He had that morning seen them, and in addi- tion to the hand rail on the right hand side, there was as one approached the top a partition, which was some sort of protection. The treads of the steps were not worn as much as he expected to find them from the evi- dence which bad been given; they were patched with wood, which ran fairly parallel with the treads, and he did not think the stairs were quite so dangerous as they had been said to be. The fact remained, however, that they were very slippery indeed. With reference to the "death trap," as it had been termed, it was a dangerous thing to have that hole at the bottom of the stairs, and he did not think he should ask a servant of his to go up and down them under the circumstances. If a person slipped—and the tendency to slip was apparent—there was nothing but a fall down the stairs into the cellar, a man could not fail to fall into the cellar, as tbere was no turn in the stairs. With reference to the Infirmary, his treatment there had been brought into question as a kind of side issue. But the jury had to decide on a matter of fact. They had heard what Drs. Cannell and Smith had to say. If the jury thought the deceased had come to his death from shock in consequence of the fall, they would be justified in attaching inch a pre-entment as they might think fit in connection with the condition of the premises. If they wished to make any suggestion about the deceased's treatment at the Infirmary, well and good ; but he (the Coroner) thought that after the discussion which had taken place, the Infirmary authori- ties were the proper people to take into consideration,' any alleged neglect of duty. He suggested, though he did not dictate, that the jury had better confine them- selves to the cause of death. After some consideration in private, the jury came to the following conclusion, which was read by the fore- man:—" That the opinion of the jury is that the man (deceased) was not drunk ; also that his death was brought about by falling into the cellar, and that Mr. Burgess is greatly to blame for allowing the aperture to be without a cover. The jury are of opinion that the Infirmary doctor acted imprudently in refusing the man admission." The Coroner then recorded a verdict of "Accidental death," and added the presentment of the jury as ex- pressed above.

Michael Egan, for intentionally committing grievous bodily harm on Martha Myers, at the Children's Shelter, Islington-square, was sentenced to four months' hard labour. Robert Richardson, charged with having feloni- ously killed Jeffrey Lomax, at Heywood, May Ist, was discharged. The affair occurred during a 'wrestling match, in which Lomax's neck was broken. Patrick Dunn, for the manslaughter of Malachi Dooley, at Liver- pool, on March 20th, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude, and his brother John, in connection with the same offence, to twelve months' hard labour.
A TIRED TRAVELLER'S TALE.-NO. 2. _

_ Oh, dear! Also confound it!! Likewise be jabers !! ! More canal, more sand, and more sleepers. I had thought to escape another such journey as the Runcorn one of the other week, but stern fate pursued, and again I am fairly in it. I had just been bumming, in fancied security, a classical verse that runs something as follows : Did you ever catch a weasel asleep; Did you ever with a sprat catch a whale; Did you ever, in a word, catch a little dicky-bird With a little pinch of salt upon its tail? Then marching orders came to hand. I hadn't meant to be easily caught, but couldn't wriggle out of it, so went. Now, lam about to apply for my summer vacation—one must have a rest. If there is any consolation in a matter of this kind, however, it is to meet someone else who seems as hard fixed as yourself. This has been the case this week. I was pottering about Latchford way, when I happened across Mr. George Ingoe, one of the superintendents of the National Telephone Company, who always seems to be hopping from one section to another. He tells me that the Company have in connection with the works about 100 miles of wire in use; but when he makes light of a " few miles," walk on the canal, which is such a serious matter to other people, lam rather disgusted. Its an every- day matter with Mr. Ingoe, but perhaps he hasn't any corns, which has a good deal to do with the case, dear boys. After all, there is more to be seen, take it on the whole, between Warrington and Warburton than between Warrington and Runcorn, the route of my last visit, and the walk is not so tiresome. To start with, you can take train from Bank Quay. to Latch- ford, and save a mile without missing the canal. You see, you can look out of the carriage window and take flying notes, so to speak. Going over the sleepers in this way is different to the other way, and more pleasant. As the train whirls towards Latchford, the paraphernalia of the contractors can be seen in the fields alongside, and you just get a glance at the bridge that is being built to span Wash-lane, which is fast approaching completion. As the train slows, it is noticed that the bridge which crosses Grappenhall-road near Latchford station is also nearly completed. It has already taken on the look of a very fine massive stone structure. From Latchford to Thelwall operations are going on at a great pace. Immediately behind Latchford Station a steam navvy is just now engaged, and, also near the station, a very pretty little office is being built. Judging from an outside look, it will when finished be one of the prettiest of the wooden erections on the canal works. I casually learn that it is for the use and convenience of Mr. John Price, who has for some time been in ckarge of the section here, but who, I incidentally gather, has recently been appointed to overlook the works from Thel- wall to Eastham, a very big job indeed. Mr. Price is unusually well liked by his subordinates, with whom I wish to take the opportunity of joining in wishing him every success in the extended sphere that his labours will now have. Mr. Hewitt has been placed in charge of the Thelwall section, in succession to Mr. Price. The locks at Latchford are progressing by leaps and bounds, and their con- struction affords one of the most interesting sights on the canal, as viewed from the top of the immense cutting. Work in connection with the sluices is also claiminga good deal of attention at the hands of those concerned in building the looks, and the piers which are to support the railway bridge over the canal are growing fast. Up to water level these piers are composed of very large blocks of Manley sandstone • above they are of red bricks, faced with blue brick„, set in cement, and it will be interesting to learn that a single layer of one pier absorbs from 4,000 to 6,000 bricks, each pier requiring about one and a half million bricks to complete it! In this connection, it may be mentioned that some distance further along the cutting immense quantities of bricks are being turned out at the brick-yard on Statham meadows, to be used in the building of bridges, and other works incidental to the cutting of the waterway. As you walk on the new road leading from Latch- ford to the offices at Morrisbrook, some idea can be obtained of the change that will be brought about in the appearance of this part of Cheshire. What with new roads, new bridges, and railway devia- tions, the change will be somewhat startling, and a natural accompaniment of the importation of so much labour into the neighbourhood, formerly so quiet and rustic, is observed in the springing up in different directions, almost as if by magic, of neat rows and terraces of comfortable looking brick dwelling-houses. One of the rows has received the appropriate name of Ship Canal View. These bonzes at present, it is to be presumed, are mostly L occupied by the sturdy toilers who make the • accomplishment of these great undertakings pos- sible, but when their task here is finished, and they

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The Congregationalists began their May meetings on Monday. In the afternoon a special prayer meeting was held in the Memorial Hall, the Rev. Dr. Falding presiding. The business meeting fol- lowed in the evening, when the chairman and Com- mittee were balloted for. At the annual assembly of the Congregational Union in London, on Tuesday, the address of the Chairman (the Rev. Thomas Green, of Ashton-under-Lyne) was delivered. In it the subject of "Independency and the Church of the Future" was dealt with, it being claimed that Independency more than any other branch of the Church of Christ had in itself the principles which must mould the Church of the days tocome. In the first ballot for chai:man none of the candidates had an absolute majority of votes, and accordingly a second ballot was necessary. In the first ballot the Rev. Dr. Brown received 343, Rev. Griffith John 189, and Principal Carr 88. In the second ballot Rev. Dr. Brown, of Bedford, was elected by 632 out of 669 votes cast. The Rev. Dr. John Brown is the chairman of the Bedfordshire ' Union of Independent and Baptist Churches, and is the minister of Bunyan Old Meeting, Bedford, where so long ago as 1650 a church was formed. Dr. Brown settled in Bedford in 1864. His " Life of John Bunyan," which occupied him many years, gained for him the distinction of D.D. from Yale University. Dr. Brown entered the Congregational ministry in 1835. He was educated at Lancashire Independent College. A conference of ministers and delegates attending the meeting of the 'Congregational Union held on Thursday at the City Temple, London, adopted a resolution in favour of free education, with the safeguard that this education should be accompanied by popular repre- sentative control in all schools aided from the public funds.

div.head: STRONGEST MAN KILLED.
div.p: THE STRONGEST MAN KILLED.

A rival of the "strongest man on earth," named Henri 'Poch, who was celebrated as an athlete at French aria Belgian fairs, has lately met with a fatal Accident. He was firing a cannon, which he carried on his shoulders, when the gun exploded, and killed Toch on the spot. The departed mountebank was a great favourite at the Paris Gingerbread Fair, which he generally attended in his capacity as a champion-wrestler. He invariably threw his opponents, who included a powerful fellow called the " Man with the iron mask," and an equally herculean person named Bazin, both of whoehad to bite the dust before the formidable biceps of Toch, who, , owing to his prowess and muscle, was entitled the ' "Rampart of the North."

SHOPPING IN SEDAN CHAIRS ONE HUNDRED YEARS QUEEN CHARLOTTE'S VISIT TO PEARS' FOR SOAP FOR HER (Uproduation of an old print qf the period.)

have gone, as no doubt they will, to work on some -other large contract, t hese brick d we:in will not long be empty. When ocan-E.Tiiiii-rittz are navigating past, and manufactories are syring- ing up on the banks of the Ship Canal, there w.II be plenty of demand for these and other residences. At least, we will hope so. As you pass along there is a good deal of active work going on in the cutting, the bottom of which is littered with cumbersome rocks. There is a homely look about Morris Brook, where so many erections of wood have been put up. Perhaps it is the presence of the little mission church that makes one feel this, or perhaps it is the thought of a rest in the coffee-room. This latter is one of the features of the canal works. It is a large wooden building, strongly constructed and neatly finished, and is 80 feet leng by 25 feet wide. Mr. George Mannirg, i who is in charge of it, and who, it may ncidentally be remarked, on Sunday week opened a new mission-room at Rixten, seems to take a good deal of interest in the welfare of the navvies and their • families,as well as in paying attention to the visitors, distinguished or otherwise, who may happen to i drop n there for refreshment. Not long since Mr. Manning, with the co-operation of some of the "heads" in this neighbourhood, succeeded in es- tablishing a Mechrinics' Instituteatthe Coffee-room, which is doing exceadingly well, there being a good number of members and a fair amount of money in hand. The room is divided into three portions. The first one comprises the quarters of t'- • Mechanics' Institute, where there are means for playing bagatelle, chess, and dominoes, and where a supply of daily and weekly tapers is provided for the use of the members. The central portion is devoted to the uses of the Coffee Tavern proper, and here meals are provided both for workmen and visitors, and at the other end of the room there is a quoit ground. Quoit-playing is a favourite pastime in the navvy world, and in wet weather the advantage of a ground under shelter is appreciated. A new vestibule has been added to the Institute part of the building. In connection with the Institute, it should be remembered, there is also a library, the books comprising which have mostly been given by people resident in Warrington and the neignbourhood. There is, of course, room for more if any lady or gentleman feels inclined to be generous in this respect. It is a pleasing fact, which is met with on all sections of the works, bar none, that a deal of attention is always paid to the well-being of the children, and of the adults, too, for the matter of that. The former have good day and Sunday school accommodation and teaching, and among the latter healthful recreation is encou- raged in the way of the formation of football, cricket, and quoit clubs. On Saturday a match was played between the club of the No. 6 (Thelwall) section, and a Grappenhall club, s which resulted in a win for the former by 58 to 36 runs, and on the same day there was a quoit match between teams representative of the same sections. As regards looking after the little ones, I am delighted to add that, at the instance, I believe of Mr. Walker's executors, arrangements are in progress by which there will be a gathering, on Whit-Monday, of chil- dren from different sections. It will be held in the neighbourhood of Thelwall ; some 600 or 700 , youngsters are expected to be present, and if the weather is fine, as we all hope it will, they will en- joy themselves as only youngsters can. The child- ren will be taken to a &id at Wash-lane, and Mr. Manning will provide the feed indispensable. Other and similar gatherings are to be held at different points, and it is expected that in all over 2,000 children will in this manner be entertained. From Morris Brook to Warburton, by way of the route line, is a pretty stiff journey, unless you do it on ansengine or in a saloon carriage, which never falls to my lot. The sleeper difficulty is again ex- perienced, and as it is rather painful to recall, and there is not much to be seen until Warburton is reached, this portion of the walk may as well be passed over without much comment. Great changes have taken place at and about Warburton since the works began, and part of the cutting here is at a rather interesting stage, though there is not quite so much doing in the way of actual work as 3ne would have expected. A little west of the Warbur- ton cutting the erection has been commenced, by Messrs. Fleming and Fergusson, of Paisley, of a pontoon dredger. It is to be of such formidable pro- portions that, as it will not be able to pass under the paybridge at Warburton, or the temporary bridge near Riaton, it has to be erected where it will be first needed. It will dredge with an endless chain of buckets, somewhat on the principle of the French and German navvies. The buckets, which number 36, are of great strength, each weighing about 14cwt. A little further on in the direction of Cottonopolis is the Irlam lock cutting, which is stated to be just now the scene of very busy oper- ations, though I did not penetrate quite so far. Two or three American navvies are at work there, and excavations have also been commenced for the con- struction of the sluices to the Irlam by-wash. The first arch of the Cadishead Viaduct has been fitted with its timber centres, and the second one is being rapidly erected. As soon as thesetemporary wooden erections are up, the work of throwing the brick arches over will be proceeded with. Back from Warburton to Warrington is an easy trip, if you combine road and rail. The keepers of the bridge still collect the halfpennies of the wayfarers, and do what business there is to be picked up in the way of "incidentals," such as the selling of light refreshments and the provision of teas for visitors. The country is looking beautilul, and it is a pleasant stride through the lanes to Heatley sta- tion, whence there is a good service of trains to Warrington. Taken on the whole the walk just finished is a nice one enough, but for the average sinner it is just a little bit too far. Anyone with a great desire to see the Canal works hereabouts, would, on the one band, be well advised to go as far as Moore and then return, or, on the other hand, to go as far as Thelma], and do aitto. Thus you escape being dreadfully done up, and you also escape the accumulation of the most destructive kind of appetite one ever heard of.

div.head: GERMANY ARMY.
div.p: THE GERMANY ARMY.

The German Parliament spent some hours on Wednesday in debating the new Army Bill. Marshall Von Moltke, speaking in support of the bill, said he had full confid- ence in the pacific intentions of Germany's neighbours, but, after all, the best security that the Empire could have was a strong army. Such an army would require money, " and more money ; " but the House must recollect that a full treasury would not of itself keep an enemy out of the country. Reference was made by several speakers to the advisableness of reducing the term of service with the colours, but the War Minister replied that the Govern- ment could at present make no concession on that head.

div.head: WOMEN'S LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: WOMEN'S LIBERAL FEDERATION.

The annual meeting of the Council of the Women's Liberal Federation commenced on Tuesday in London. Mrs. Theodore Fry occupied the chair, and Mrs. Glad- stone, president of the Federation, was also present. It was resolved that the Federation should take cognizance of all Bills and political proposals touching subjects likely to interest the affiliated associations, and should call up- on each association to discuss such proposals, with a view toaction that might be considered right and expe- dient. A resolution was carried in support of a Bill to make women eligible as county councillors and aldermen. In the evening the annual meeting was held under the presidency of Mrs. Gladstone. Mr. John Dillon, M.P., delivered an address. At the meeting of the Women's Liberal Federation, on Wednesday, a resolution was adopted declaring that the liquor traffic ought to be placed under popular control, and that the proposal of the government to give compensation for the extinction of licenses was unjutifiable. Some difference of opinion was expressed in the discussion of a motion declaring that the time had come when the enfranchisement of women ought to be included in the Liberal programme. In the end the reso- lution was carried, with only ten dissentients.

div.head: DUEL TO THE DEATH.
div.p: A DUEL TO THE DEATH.

Two Italians fought a duel at New York on Sunday with stilettos. Both men were expert with their weap- ons, and the combat lasted several hours. The antag- onists were in a long chamber denuded of furniture, and half a dozen of their countrymen acted as seconds. After the battle had lasted two hours a halt was called for refreshments. Both men had several flesh wounds, but their appetites were keen and they ate a hearty meal sitting opposite each other, their seconds dividing them. Then a cigarette was smoked and the fight resumed. The men fought with the utmost caution for some time, un- til finally they closed and both began to stab each other I repeatedly until they fell to the ground exhausted and a mass of wounds. They were wrapt in blankets and a.r- ried to a hospital, where they died while being examined by the doctors. One of the men was stabbed in the eye, a part of the dagger remaining in his brain; the other man had no fewer than 14 stabs in his stomach. The witnesses of the affair have been arrested for complicity in murder. They are all Italian labourers of humble rank, who emigrated together from Leghorn.

div.head: SHOCKING MURDER AT STOCKTON-ON-
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER AT STOCKTON-ON-
TEES.

-- A terrible murder was committed at Stockton-on-Tees on Sunday morning. A young man named Frederick Terry went on Saturday night to a house in Alberto.st., with an unfortunate named Sarah Merryweather, from Northallerton, and took lodgings. They were apparently sober and reered quietly. At five o'clock on Sunday morning the landlord,named Lockwood, heard the woman scream, and he rushed into the room, where he found Terry hacking the woman's throat and face with a razor. He dragged the woman out of the room and locked the door upon the prisoner. The woman vUed in a few minutes, having received dreadfui injuries to the throat. Terry, who quietly submitted to arrest, is 21 years-of age, and son of Mr. Terry, late gas manager at Croft Gas Works, near Darlington. No motive is assigned for the murder. A verdict of "Wilful murder" was returned on Mon- day, by a coroner's jury, at Stockton-on-Tees, arainst Frederick Terry, aged twenty-one. for killing Sarah Merryweather, aged nineteen, by cutting her throat, face, and chest in a shocking manner. Terry was taken before the borough magistrates, on Monday, and re- manded until Thursday.

div.head: LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.
div.p: LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.
LOCALICASES AT THE ASSIZES,

Tlietiverpool Assizes opened on Monday The following local cases have been dealt with. ST. HELENS. John Conroy (29), blacksmith, was charged with stealing a jacket, a vest, a pair of trousers, and other articles, the property of Joseph Connor, at Windle, on February Ist. Prisoner, against whom there were previous convictions, was sent to gaol for twelve months with hard labour. Martin Buckley (30), labourer, was sent to prison for six months with hard labour for unlawfully and maliciously wounding John lienry Nickson, at St. Helens, on the 26th ult. Mary Ellen Molyneux (22), who pleaded guilty to stealing a chemise, the property of John White, at Eccleston, on the Bth inst., was sent to prison for three months.
HORRIBLE WIFE MURDER BY A PUGILIST.

- - Early on Monday morning a brutal murder was com- mitted at Bradford, the victim being a woman about 30 years of age, residing in Lord-at. :Her husband, James Harrison, a pugilist, and well-known to the police, is alleged to be the person who committed the deed. It appears that shortly before five o'clock on Monday morn- ing, Harrison went to his wife's bedroom, and without saying a word to her dragged her out of bed and stabbed her with a large carvinr, knife. He then seized her by she hair, and after dragging her downstairs in the kitchen, beat in her skull with a poker. The deed was perpetrated in the presence of the murderer's three children, and some of the neighbours hearing their screams broke into the house, but Mrs. Harrison was laid dead on the floor, and presented a fearful appearance. The murderer seemed perfectly indifferent to what had taken place, and when the police arrived on the scene, he calmly gave himself up, and as he pas . along the street Coolly bid his acquaintances good most.. it.. It is statea that the two people have led a very , ppy life, and that he has upon :many occasions thn atened to kill his

wife. '1 ne prisoner James Harrison Was brought before the flradford magistrates on Monday morning, and remanded for a week. Be appeared slightly nertous, but other- wise betrayed no concern., When arrested all he said was, "We had a few words, and I could not help it." The neighbours state that he often threatened the life of his wife, and he frequently beat her. His reputation for violence was such that' none of them dared inter- fere.

A fire which raged at Shawlands, near Glasgow, throughout Wednesday night has destroyed a Nock of buildings, and the loss is estimated at £lO,OOO. No fewer than seven shops and eighteen dwellings were gutted,and the tenants of the latter are now homeless.

div.head: SOLDIERS ON THE SPREE.
div.p: SOLDIERS ON THE SPREE.

The extraordinary theft of a barrel of beer from the. Lancashire and Yorkshire station at the Altcar Range was investigated on Wednesday. at the County Magis- trates' Court in Liverpool. As the result nine privates of the 2nd Cheshire Regiment, named Wm. Mills, Row- land Meach, Wen. Davies, George Thomas, R. Catterall, Bernard Cooney, J. Woods, T. Ashford, and H. Briggs, were each ordered to pay a fine of 20s. and costs, or go to gaol for fourteen days.
THE TRIPLE, MURDER AT LIVEV POOL.

On Saturday, an inquest was opened before Mr. Brig.- house, county coroner, at Toxteth Park, Liverpool, on William Robert Charlton, aged four; Dorothy Bennett Charlton, aged two; and Barbara Bennett Charlton, aged ten months, the children of Charles Arthur Charl- ton, whose wife Leah is accused of murdering them on the evening of Thursday week, by cutting their throats with a razor, at 16, Garmoyle-st., off Smithdown-road. The inquest was adjourned until June 9, the coroner stating that the mother, who had cut her own throat. and was now in the hospital of the Smithdown-road Workhouse, was in a precarious state, and there were doubts as to her recovery. If she died in the meantime the inquiry would be resumed earlier. The funeral of the three infant victims in the Gar- moyle-road tragedy took place at Southdown-road Cemetery, on Monday. The interment was fixed for ten o'clock, and by that time a considerable crowd, com- posed mainly of respectably-dressed women residing in the neighbourhood, had gathered at the Cemetery. The father of the children, Charles A. Charlton, and his brother, were the only mourners. From the chapel to the graveside the remains were borne by three bearers, who walked in procession, each carrying a tiny coffin on his shoulder. The spectacle was indescribably melan- choly, and was the cause of a great many women in the ' crowd bursting into tears. The Rev. Francis Smith, curate of St. Clement's, Windsor-road, read the burial service. Several police constables were present, and were directed by Inspector Baxendale.

div.p: The THE Dissentient Liberals mustered • Hartington m strong force at the banquet to Banquet. Lord HARTINGTON on his recoverY from illness, which wait given in .the Crystal Palace on Tuesday evening. It showed loyalty t° leadership that they should thus signalise his re- turn to the direction of a party which, as the various bye-elections reveal, grows "fine by grees, and beautifully less." It is Lord HAIIII-NO- - who holds the Dissentients together in the House of Commons; for his opposition to Holne Rule is founded on a strong conviction that ite adoption would be injurious alike to England end to Ireland. He is not like Mr. CuAnsEaLON, who has expressed himself in favour of the Prin. elide of Home Rule, and who is in oppositioL because he cannot lead the leader of the Liberal ' party. The difference between the two wee pithily expressed by Sir WILLIAM HARCOVA, when he said Lord HARTINGTON was opposed t° HOllle Rule; whilst Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was opposed to Mr. GLADSTONE. This opposition to gr' GLADSTONE crops up whenever the member for West Brmingham speaks on political questional and it showed itself in his speech as chairman al the banquet. He said Mr. GLADSTONE'S polle9 was one of evasion and concealment, and described his followers as a " servile band" growing" ri:ore convinced the less they understand.' Liberala throughout the country do not fait to note the language of insult which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN de- liberately and persistently uses; and they are, thankful that they have found him out, and Wu" him out in time. The gods are just even to bot,' and the punishment which has been meted- out ell him is to have to take rank as a follower of 'Lord HARTINGTON. It is not many years since the member for West Birmingham was impatient Of Mr. GLADSTONE because the Liberal pace was 11° quick enough, whilst as for Lord HARTINGTOS b° had nothing but contempt for him as a Rip llart, Winkle whose Liberalism had gone to sleep. An" now Rip Van Winkle is spoken of by Mr. CHAMIO' LAIN as "our party leader" and as "a gro Englishman." It is" thus the whirligig of Tire°
I

brings in his revenges." It is due to the member for Rossendale to state that he stands where he did. He never was a° advanced Liberal, and, as he does not advance) is in the nature of things that he should find sslf high and dry in the No-man's-land which - between Liberalism and Toryism. In a few it is inevitable, as it seems to us, that Loll' HARTINGTON will be part and parcel of the Tori party—not so much because he has retreated as because he has stood still and the Tories 1101; overtaken him; for it must be remernberell' that Tories are Tories because they are alwaYS' a stage behind the Liberals. It is not alone' opposition to Home Rule which is the matter with Lord HARTINGTON ; it is such things "unauthorised programmes," and unauthoriee' leaders of which he has a horror; and Mr. enAr BERLAIN must have felt uncomfortable when heard his lordship thus deliver himself : I have stated some of the reasons for which oar party was formed—some of the reasons winell„t induce us to think that we could never rejoin 0. old leaders and our old party. (Cheers.) There other reasons which I think lead us to view tn, prospect with equanimity. Ido not know for O. ...11" who are the leaders of that party,or what its fttur,A. policy is likely to be. I know that some o party with whom I have had the honour of votiuri in past times will, if the Liberal party regef2l„t -power, resume certain offices under the Crown; I don't know—l think it is very hard to known are the men who will have the real guidance direction of the future of the Home Rule (Hear, hear.) hear.) I don't by any means venture to 00,1 demn all the new developments of Liberalism whim.° seem to be in many respects not only far in advsls„ but widely separated from those principles wb_."'" hitherto it has been the pride of the Libera' palZ, to adopt. But I don't deny that our concerf tion of politics, the conception of politics 0 my generation, of my age—may not be a CO plete conception of the needs and wants of thir great and growing community. It may be that times to come our preconceived notions of the fuer; tions of government may have to be large' extended. It may be that we shall find' that the State can safely perform many fungtions Whi every Liberal of the old school had always tboug,, it had much better abstain from interfering vi',.l"h; but I only ask that when this policy becomes rt accepted policy of the Liberal party some furtue., information shall be given us than has ever yet beet; furnished to us. What are the aims and objecte,d which they are tending, and what are the ge,t",e1,73 measures by which those aims and objects W'll promoted? Further, I ask whether, when this t Radicalism is to become the effective creed of tit, party, its measures should be carried into effect " men who have faith in them. Lord HARTINGTON never had any sympathy vilmr "The Radical Programme" as promulgated, 'cit Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. He has no sympathy wit' now when it is deserted by Mr. CHABlesabAl'io He is a Whig; he always was a Whig; aria it, the fate of Whigs who cannot "move on" absorbed in the Tory party. It is suggestive that, however it may be with less observant followers, the leader of n, Dissentients sees that there is a possibility of gor% Rule being adopted. He says :—" We have/ at ail events, secured this, that if the countrY ever ~cif: accept the Home Rule policy—(" never ")---'"7,„ only accept it after it has been adequately enma sidered and discussed throughout the countrly no measure of Home Rule will ever be forced)!P might have been the case, on an unprepared t ment and unprepared constituencies." We "7:i begrudge Lord HARTINGTON'S aCknOWledgraem' _ this service, for the delay has led to the demand for Home Rule all round. His Lordship practic admits this in his reference to Mr. AstirlTll recent speech which, he said, "points to the cona: stitution of four Parliaments for Englan._, Scotland, Ireland and Wales, with an 1na13e7.,,. view of every task of magnitude ;but it is not the Liberal way of looking at things. If difficulties arise, and they are continually arising, they are not to he shirked; they are to be grappled with and surmounted. Lord HARTINGTON, LordSALISBITRY, and Lord DERBY have made much, and they have a right to make much, of the fact that the reten- tion of the Irish members in Westminstbr is objectionable in that it gives them a share in con- trolling- English domestic affairs in addition to I'"virg the Control of their own. We have fore- °Oll from the first that an arrangement of this kind could. not be permanent, and we have fore- aeen, too, that "the way 04 " was to extend the Principle of Home Rule to England, and Scotland, and Wales, as well as to Ireland. That is the answer to the Dissentient and Tory objection, and it is a complete answer. Lord HARTINGTON Says in effect it cannot be done—it is impossible. But that remains to be seen. The " impossible " iU politics has been accomplished a hundred times. TO raise the cry of "impossible" is the Tory way of aPProaching things. The Liberal way is to disre- gard the Word, and get the thing done. And it Will be done in this case.

MR. STANLEY has been giving his England views on what may be called the Ad Africa' scramble for Africa; and he seems to think England is half-a-sleep upon the subject, While Germany is wide-awake. He confesses that himself has been the means in a large measure of the Germans taking to the colonisation of East Africa. He lectured in Germany in 1885, and the • People paid attention to him; but that was after lecturing in England when his 'proposals were treated with apathy. It is evident that Mr. STANLEy regards the present Government as ready te give away the Queen's Crown, if Germany Should take it into her head to ask for it. He tn.3's knVire are in a happy vein of giving. Germany "rs right well how to ask. lam only surprised that: she does not ask more. Look at the question Njaro. The young Emperor would like .s.,_ Or a sanatorium. He is interested. in the florai qua the fauna. '0 yes, tell Hatzfeldt to ask for t.' COunt Hatzfeldt goes to the Foreign Office, is re- ceived with gt ntle courtesy by a Secretary of State :iv_no chiefly desires to be left in peace on a subject r_Which the country is not interested. 'The young. raPer,or is attracted by the flowers of Kilinia ti.,nro• `No doubt; yes, they are very interesting.' the would like to have the mountain included in Such, and territory," By all means, 'certainly.', "'n„ueni, and the thing is done. Why, if Spam knew well as Germany how to ask, she would have .„`1,4 Gibraltar long ago. If France knew how tp :4!1, she would have Egypt; if Russia knew how to o'7, she might get India. Fortunately for us, only rniany so far understands the ,art in its perfec- tion. German methods are not our methods. , • 'ir• STANLEY holds that there is a vast territory to be taken possession of by England in Central Africa, if England, like Germaily" will be wise enough to make up her mind He says :—"The question lies now once more before the country. In the course of our late expedition we made trea- ties for England with all the chiefs 'to the very lhaaits of the Congo territory." But will this coun- try follow the matter up, and take possession these treaties? Or, will she continue the P°liey of letting things slide? There is appar- ently a plentiful lack of decision on the part of those who are at the head of affairs. It i 8 not unlikely that Lord SALISBURY finds Iniuself unequal to the task of combining the duties of oreign Secretary and Prime Minister, and that 'foreign, and colonial affairs are suffering in conse- ;:luence. The two posts certainly ought not to be held for any length of time by one person. In B:43'ing this we do not wish it to be understood that Mr. STANLEY is necessarily right in urging England 4:111t° further conquests in Africa. It must not bo lost sight of that there is a wide difference be- , tween England and Germany; the latter country In I,as but commencing a career of colonisation; while e forifler is the holder of possessions in every rju. arter of the globe. An empire may become too big tbe handled, and may break up in conse- . cslue!nee• • Still so far as Africa is concerned, Mr. „Unlnv is the man who above all others under- 4ands the subject. What he says and what he 44,,civises should be carefully weighed. It is, one 'Lung to leave Central Africa to other countries, after due consideration of all that it involves, and . quite another to let the question slide through Ignorance and indifference. What are we about? th=e British lion sleeping just now with both ()las shut?

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
We have"a letter to hand from Mr. Whitham— " Chiefly Personal "—which will appear in our next issue.
We are unable to find room for all the letters on the Romish controversy, but our correspondents will see that we have devoted considerable space to the question.

Is is stated that during a thunderstorm, the other day, the Eiffel Tower was struck no fewer than six times; and that the tower shuddered through all its length. We should think so. It is very much like a thundering notice to quit.

A contemporary says:—" A large oak tree in the cemetery at Salem, Virginia, was split by lightning last week, exposing a silver teapot which ccntained the skull of a child. The date on the teapot was 1S:28. Its history is a mystery." . Just so; but we should say there is an inventive penny-a-liner somewhere in America who &mid explain the mystery.

The Secretary of State for War announced on Monday, that the Volunteers are to be suitably equipped, or allowed 12s. per man for the purpose. "Better late than never." Bub why should Mr. Stanhope suggest that the public should piece out what the Government are doing ? We do not want to make beggar-men of our Volunteer Officers. Let us do the thing decently and in order whilst we are about it.

The report is enrrent in g.ermany that the British Government have intimated to the German Government that there is no chance of carrying out the London Sugar Convention. There has been a pretence in this country that the bill was not dead but sleeping, but it would seem now to be acknowledged that there is no life in it. The best thing about the Sugar Bounty Bill is the end of it. It was a large mouthful of Protection, and couldn't be swallowed.

People who are interested in Stanley and his achievements would do well to secure, if they can, a copy of ." The Graphic " Stanley number. Besides giving an interesting account of the great explorer's career, it contains portraits of him and his officers, and of Emin Pasha. There is a map of the route, an ancient map of Africa, and views of prin- cipal scenes and incidents. The coloured supple- ments are, as might be expected.splendid specimens of fine-art printing.

• A capital representation of the Lord Mayor's Show has been issued by Messrs. Crosfield and Sons as a means of advertising "Perfection Soap," It introduces the Metropolitan Police, Lancers, Watermen, Beefeaters, Guards, Rifle Brigade and the Lord Mayor's carriage and escort. Brigade, the various costumes are reproduced in celour, the effect is most brilliant. It is altogether a really admirable specimen of chromo-lithography ; and proves a great source of attraction wherever it is exhibited.

The Government, on Thursday night, carried the second reading of their Compensation Bill by a majority of 73; but that does not mean that the struggle is ended—it is simply begun. There will be meetings now all through the kingdom—meet- ings not of temperance bodies alone, but of the public generally, for the bill involves the taxing of the public for the benefit of rich brewers. If they are willing to bleed fo;brewers, well and good ; but let them do it with ther eyes open.

Mt. Gladstone thoroughly exposed the weakness of the bill on Thursday night. Referring to the argument that slave-holders had been compensated he said, (amid laughter and cheers :)--" As allusion has been made to West India compensation, I should like to know what Parliament would have said to West India compensation if twenty millions had been placed in the hands of a public authority to go round amongst the West India proprietors and emancipate such of the slaves as they could satisfy proprietors they did not need."

In another portion of his speech, Mr. Gladstone described the measure as "a bill for buying out an extremely small portion of the publicans upon those terms which the publipans themselves may fix; " and he estimates that it would take 700 years to extinguish all licenses at the rate proposed by the Government. Sir Wilfrid Lawson struck even harder at the scheme when he said it was " notking more or less than black-mail levied on the people to put in the pockets of the political supporters of the Government." Will the public stand this black-mail? That is the question.

The House of Commons is not yet ripe for restricting actions for breach of promise. At Tues- day's evening sitting, Sir R. Lethbridge rose to move, "That in the opinion of this ifouse the action of breach of promise of marriage ought to be abolished, except in case where actual pecuni- ary less had been incurred by reason of the promise, the damages being limited to such pecuniary loss." But when the House came to be counted it was found that the number was below the magical forty; and the motion came to an untimely end.

There is another epidemic of Scarlet fever in St. Helens' and it is suggested that schools in the district more particularly affected should be closed for a month. It is a serious step to take; but it is more serious still to go on'until the epidemic has spread to every part of the town. Already there have been seven deaths. Families which the disease has attacked would do well to carefully observe and rigidly adhere to the instructions of the Medical Officer of Health. It is difficult to beat out the enemy unless there is co-operation in every quarter.

The Princess Mary of Cambridge was announced to distribute the prizes, on Monday, at an Exeter Hall gathering of the supporters of the Ragged School Union. But tIA) Princess was late, and a chorus was repeated by way of killing time. When Princess Mary arrived, the children had approached an item on the ptograrame entitled "Wake up, Mary ;" and, what gave point to the piece, it illustrated the evils of lack of punctuality. The Chairman, Lord Kinnard, thought it best to skip' the item, but there was a hearty laugh for all that. "Wake up, Mary," will not be forgotten just' yet. ,

£40,000 is being offered by French Jews for the copy of the Hebrew Bible in the possession of the Pope. It is not for sale; but why such a high figure? The growing custom of giving thousands of pounds for things not intrinsically worth as many shillings, is a sign of wealth, and of the cor- ruption of wealth. £40,000 at 4 per cent, would bring in £1,600 a year, and properly applied it would help to improve the condition of some of the thousands of Jews who are being "sweated" almost out of existence in all the great centres of in- dustry. And so of pictures, pottery, and furni- ture. Tremendously high prices are a fraud, and help in the long run to grind the faces of the poor.

The Duke of Argyll .is amongst the illiberal Liberals who have gone over to the enemy, be- cause of their hatred of interference with the divine rights of property. He had his reasons, for the Highland Land Court are now dealing with the property of his Grace. "They have re- duced the rents of the crofters on the Mull pro- perty by 39 per cent., and have wiped off two- thirds of the rent in arrear. The Duke's crofting tenants residing on the well-known tourist resort of the island of lona have had their rents reduced 27 pa cent." His Grace has been squeezing out,

ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

Robert Flarrop-al-ndAi'dijir- Lit-tier,- bricklayers, were engaged pointing a house in Brunswick-st., when the scaffolding upon which they were standing gave way, and they were precipitated to the ground. Harrop's left leg was fractured and he sustained a severe shock to the system and Littler was also badly injuied. Dr. Mangan is attending to the injured men.

div.head: DRAGOON GI7ARDS AT WIDNES.
div.p: DRAGOON GI7ARDS AT WIDNES.

On Monday a detachment of the sth Dragoon Guards, on their way from Seaforth to• Aldershot, arrived in Widnes, where they were billeted for the night. It was originally intended to pass through Widnes and cross the Mersey by Runcorn Bridge, but this was found impracti- cable, and on Tuesday morning the men 45 in number, proceeded via Warrington to Middlewich.

div.head: IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE, WIDNES.
div.p: IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE, WIDNES.

The weekly meeting of the T. P. O'Connor Branch, was held on Sunday, Mr. P. Horan in the chair. „A letter was read from the assistant secretary of the League, Roscommon, Ireland, acknowledging a Bs,, the proceeds of a concert, held in Widnes, for the benefit of Miss B. Coleman, Belanagare, who, it was alleged, had been un- justly evicted from her home. A vote of condolence with the relatives of the late Mr. P. Byrne, of Liverpool, was carried unanimously. .

PEERS ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY, WIDNES. The first annual meeting was held in Lacey-st. school- room, on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. T. Sadler. The directors, in their report, state the profit on the year's working to be £46 14s. 7p., and they recom- mended that a bonus of one shilling per share be given on all paid up shares, and the balance of £34 3s. Md. carried to the Reserve Fund. The balance sheet was, adopted. The retiring directors Messrs. Thmas Sadler, John Thomas, John Jackson, and Samuel Sadler, were re-elected. The auditor, Mr. S. Hoyle, was also re-ap- pointed. _ _ _

PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. ' The anniversary was celebrated on Sunday, when special services were held in the Chapel in Greenway- road. The pulpit was occupied morning and evening by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, of Southport, and in the after- noon by the Rev. John Simpson of Bethesda Congrega- tional Church. Specially selected music was sung at each service, and there were good congregations. On Monday evening a public meeting was held in the chapel under the presidency of the Rev. C. Finch, and addresses were delivered by the Revs. J. Judson, J. D. Bray, and H. Davenport. Collections were made at each service,in aid of the funds. SUMMER Fenno:vs, now showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. ANOTHER EXPLOSIVE STORE FOR RUNCORN, At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Reynolds, an application was made by Mr. Davenport, on behalf of the exe- cutors of Mr. T. A. Walker, for a license to goable them to keep explosives in a store erected in a 11. Pd at Hatton. near Marsh Farm. The application was made under Divisiou C, which would enable Mr. Knott to keep 2,0001b5. weight of mixed explosives, which were in- tended to be used on the Ship Canal.—Superintendent Large said he had inspected the store and he found it well constructed and in accordance withtlae Act of Parlia- ment. It was 1,000 yards from any dwelling, while it was only necessary to be 100 yards. The license was granted. SELF-WILLED TO DESTRUCTION AT WIDNES. On Saturday, at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, held 'am inquest on the body of Henry Morgan, 67 years of age, who was killed on Thursday evening. The deceased was employed as an "odd man" at the Commercial Hotel, Widnes Marsh, and for the purpose of whitewashing the exterior walls of the kitchen, he had constructed a scaffold con- sisting of two planks. Mr. Radley, the landlord, told him the scaffold was "nothing but a trap," and forbade him to go upon it.—Two jurymen stated that on the morning of the accident they told the deceased the scaf- fold was not safe. He was a man addicted to drink, but ' was quite sober at the time. He was very self-willed.—' A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. -trY44lllO WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday after- noon, and there were present Messrs. H. Wade Deacon, J. H. Lee, F. H. Pankhurst, D. J. Brookes, W. Sadler, J. Morrison, S. Sadler, J. Robinson, J. T. Men (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian). On the proposition of Mr. Pankhurst. seconded by Mr. W. Sadler, Mr. Deacon was unanimously re-elected chairman for the ensuing year. The Librarian reported that during April the attendance at the library had been 12,031, or a daily average of 501, against 505 for the same month last year. There had been 4,375 books issued during themonth,a daily average of 182. It was decided to get 6,000 cards printed and distributed amongst the householders, stating that the library was free, and books could be borrowed without payment, so long as the rules were adhered to. RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.

By the kindness of Mr. J. E. Langshaw, the sec., we are enabled to give a few details of the phenomenal suc- cess of the Runcorn Football Club during the past season. The first team has played 36 matches, of which 29 were won, three drawn, and four lost, the total scores were Runcorn, 79 goals, 77 tries, 116 minors ; opponents 12 goals, 23 tries, and 56 minors, being a majority in favour of Runcorn of 67 goals, 49 tries, and 60 minors. No. fewer than 150 tries were scored by Runcorn, of which Cromp- ton obtained 45, Davies 37, P. Riley 11, H. Hughes 9, J. Gayter 7, W. Faulkner 5, A. Hampson 5, W. Broady 6, and W. F. Hancock 3; T. Woods, S. Abrams, W. H. Cawley, R. Dolan, W. Hughes, and J. Davies were re- sponsible for two each. and J. Brazendaye, Rev. G. H. Kingstone, W. Shaw, Geo. Lee, and H. May each scored one. Crompton dropped four goals and Broady one. It will be observed that of the tries scored, 73 were con- verted into goals, a capital average for which Crompton is principally to be thanked. Already arrangements have been made for next season, for which a strong list of fixtures have been made, including matches with Bradford, Swinton, Salford,l3roughton, Leeds St. John's, Wigan, Birkenhead Park, Liverpool Pld Boys, New ' Brighton, Broughton Rangers, Rochdale Hornets, Burton- on-Trent, Old Edwardians,Sale, Tuebrook, and Stockport. The annual nieeting of members will be held on Tuesday. next, in the large room at Mr. A. Riley's Cafe, Bridge-st. SUMMER FAsaroNs, now showing at Ss W. Durrow s, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
