div.head: MORE MAGIbTRITES AT WIDNES.
div.p: MORE MAGIbTRITES AT WIDNES.

There were about 40 cases oa the list at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, but only Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., ap- pearedon the Bench. He adjudicated on those matters with which one magistrate could deal i and then waited an hour and a half for a scond magistrate to turn up, but although the police scoured the town another justice of the peace could not be found, and the cases had to be adjourned. Mr. Gaskell expressed his regret for the great inconvenience caused to a large number of persons. —Mr. J. C. Gamble was on the,rota:for the thy, and Mr. Gaskeli was offirinting for Air. .Deacon. When will the Chancellor of the Duchy alter this state of things, by appointing more magistrates who reside in the locality.? RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE AND THE COMPENSATION

PROPOSALS OF THE GOVERNMENT. At the usual fortnightly meeting of tha above Order on Saturday last, there was an animated discussion on Mr. Goschen's scheme of compensation in which the following members took part t—Mossrs, IV. BisbroWn. Thomas Ceoke, Thomas Hecsom; Thomas Holt and S. Henderson. It was said that the action of the Govern- ment in this matter should meet with the strenuous opposition of every temperance reformer. , The Object was to give legislative sanction to the principle of com- pensation, a principle which the country so promptly rejected two years ago. The following resolution was carried—" That this meeting of the Sons of Temperance earnestly request J. 'l'. Brunner, Esq.. Ml'., to vote against the Government proposals for compensating publican and givinga continuous vested interest in each annual drinfc license." Mr. Thomas Whyte occupied the chair.

iIIUSING BURGLARY AT BUNCOUN. A boatman named John Hilyar was brought before Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst at itundorn Police Court, yeSter- day, charged with burglariouslv breaking; and entering the shop of George Davidson, pork hi:Leber, Church-st., and stealing six meat pies worth 3.. 61. About mid- night.; on Thursday, Davidsuri'...s(;pviint_irl heard Some person try the door and then smisii t .1, i.-irul?w of the shop. She raised an alarm, and without his shoes went in search of the burglar. He found the prisoner concealed in an entry eating a pie and he seized him, but ti e prisoner proved too strong for him and made his escape. Davidson went in pursuit and saw the prisoner descend the steps on Doctor's Bridge, and after- wards heard a splash. On arriving on the canal bank, he fOund the prisoner in the water, and clinging to the side. He appealed to Davidson to pull him out •but the litter replied "No, you are where you ought to be," and he kept him in his perilous position until the arrival of, P.C. Edmonds, who conveyed the half-drowned boatman to the lock-up. The prisoner who has been convicted of felony on several occasions, was ' committed to the Assizes for trial.
RETIREMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT JOHNSTONE, OF WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Mr. C. H. Lewin (deputy magistrate's clerk),said that was the last occasion Superintendent Johnstone would appear in that court in an official capacity. They all very much regret- ted the circumstances under which he was compelled to retire, namely, the state of his health, and he would carry with him in his retirement the good wishes, not only of himself and the Bench, but the whole community. During the three years Superintendent Johnston o had been located in this division they had worked most har- moniously together. --Mr. J. W. Knowles said during Superintendent Johnstone's time there had been no un- pleasant scenes in court or out of it,and on behalf of him- self and the other solicitors in the town, he hoped that Mr. Johnstone might live long in the roll eenr.-nt which he had so well earned and that his successor might be as able and worthy a man.—Mr. H. (*asked, kin., the only magistrate present, added his good wishes to those of Mr. Lewin and Mr. Knowles. Mr. Johnstone was retir- ing after a very long service in the county, and he was ' retiring with the sympathy and good w?shes, not only of the Bench, awl all connected with the court, but with the good wishes of his fellow townsmen in Widnes. He had only heard One expression of opinion withimgardto his services in the town and that was that he had given universal satisfaction in every way. He hoped he might have many years before him to enjoy in good health, his well-earned retirement.—Superintendent Johnstone said he felt very grateful to them for their kind expressions. He was sure he had not done anything more than was fair and square between man and man, and he did not think he deserved half the praise he had got for it. He was sorry that he had come to Widnes in his declining health instead of in the vigour of his manhood, when he could have served them better. He asked them to accept his best thanks for their good wishes. (Applause.)— Inspector Noblett, of Over Darwen, has been appointed by the joint committee of the County Council to succeed Mr. Johnstone, on the recommendation of Colonel Moorsom. _ . _
TEASELLING TRUNlCS.—Gartand, Ironnion;er, 51, Bridge- st.. Warrington. , ANOTHER. VICTIM IN WESTON POINT CANAL.

The Coroner, Mr. J. E. Worsley, on, Thursday after- noon held an inquest at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on the body of Triofnas Quirke, an able-bodied seaman, 20 veers of ago, a native of Port Erin, and a hand on board the schooner Goldsecker.—Edward Stevens, mate on the vessel, which is moored in Weston Point Docks, said he last saw the deceased alive on Friday night, at half-past eight. Clara Marsh, landlady of the Sailors Home, Regent-st.. Runcorn, said the deceased came to her house on Friday night about half-past nine. He and five others had half a gallon of ale. The deeeascd stated he would have a bed, but he afterwards changed his mind and left at half-past eleven. He was not altogether sober when he came in, having had a little drop at Weston Point, but he was right enough when he left. It was raining hard, and was very dark, and she tried to per- suade him to stay all night.—Mr. Rozenburg : Was it the distance that made you think it was not safe for him to go or was it the drink he had had P—l thought the dis- tance was long and as it was raining, and he had no need to be on board, I thought he might as well stay.—Mr. Rozenberg : Was he sober ?—Well, no sir, he was not , what I should call drunk. The deceased was a stranger to Weston Point and the road is dangerous.—PC. Hamersley deposed to finding the body of the deceased in the canal on Wednesday. There was no mark of violence and there was about 18s. in the pockets.--Witness came along the towing path about midnight on the Friday, but he did not see the deceased. It was his impression that the lamps on the other side of the canal were not lit, but he was not certain apout it.—The Coroner said he had very little doubt that the man was drunk, and that the landlady of the public-house did not want him to get into danger. He, however, left and there was no doubt that in walking to Weston Point, he accidentally fell into the canal. The road was a most dangerous one, and they had a long record of persons drowned at the particular point where the deceased's body was found. So long as that road remained so long would the jury be called together to hold these inquiries. He hadniven expression to his views en the subject before and it was unnecessary to repeat them. The facts spoke for them- selves and they ought to be eloquent enough to cause some inquiries to be made, and an alteration made.—A verdict of "Found drowned" was returned. A DROWNING MYSTERY AT WIDNES. . -

Mr. S. Brighouse, the coroner for South-West Lanca- shire, on Saturday morning held an inquest at the MerSey Hotel, Widnes, on the body of a man unknown who was found floating in the river Mersey,on Thursday evening, by a boy named John Ashton, of 108, Terrace- road. P.C. W. Robinson described the body, and the clothing upon it, which particulars have been published in this journal. There were no marks on the body that would lead to identity in the future.—A police sergeant said a very good photo had been taken of the man's fea- tures —Ajuryman said that the man's head was much battered and he might have met with foul play.—Other jurymen remarked that the body might have come in contact with a flat or with someprojecting rock.—James Ashton,flatman, of Terrace-road, said he thought he saw the deceased on the steep part of the rocks on Thursday morning about half-past ten. The deceased was talking as if he was out of his mind, and saying "Send them down here and I will drown' every—one of them." He was not a native of Widnes ; he" talked as if he came out of Cheshire." Witness again went to view the body and said he was still of opinion the deceased was the man he saw on Tfmrsday morning.—Frederick Lomax, flatman, said he was with the last witness on Thursday morning. The man he saw on Thursday sitting on the rock about two feet from the water wore a black knitted j.ket, but he could not swear that the deceased was the man. The man shouted" I have been away from home for a week, looking for work, and I have got none and they have set the bobbies on me, but send them down here and [will drown everyone." There was 8 feet of water at the feet of the man, and witness remarked to his companion "that chap's out of his mind and is going to drown himself."—The jury returned an open verdict.—A juryman (James Burrows) said the deceased had no clothing upon him, and he understood that he would be put in the coffin" stark naked," and he thought this was a very inhuman way of 4nterring the man.—The Coroner said the man ought to be decently buried. He should like the body to be naked so that the jury could see if there were any marks on the body, but afterwards the body ought to be laid out in a proper manner. The Coroner instructed P.S. Strickland to convey this expressly ta the relieving officer, and say no one would begrudge the extra cost. SUMMER Fagan/ca. now showing at J. lc W. BUTTON'S, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt.

Mr. William Dannett, who has occupied the re- sponsible position of postmaster of St. Helens, for the past four years, receiveq the gratifying intima- tion a few days ago, that he had been promoted to a more important post in the Wigan postal district. Mr. Dannett by his uniform kindness and diligence secured general , popularity among all classes with whom.he came in contact. div.head: FURIOUS DRIVING.
div.p: FURIOUS DRIVING.

At the St. Helens Town Mall, on Monday, Henry Parkinson. of Collins Green, and William Conway, of Burtouwood, were summoned ori a charge of furiously driving their, horses, attached to milk carts, in Sharp-st., t. Helens, on the 6th inst. P.C. Kilpatrick stated that the defendants were standing up in their carts lashing their horses and Conway was attempting to pass Parkinson.—The Bench remarked that the practice was a very dangerous one and fined Parkinson 7s. Gd. and costs, and Con- way 2s. 6d. and Mts. SUMMER FASHIONS now showing at J. &W. EtrFvox's, Sankey-st., Warrington.-4dvt. THE HOME IRON TEAM. For the last three weeks, the English init.' market has displayed a steadily downward tendency, and the volume of business transacted has been on a correspondingly dwindling scale. The reports re- ceived during that time with regard tO pig iron es- pecially, have been very discouraging, and the fall in prices has been marked. No. 3 Cleveland pig was pretty steady at 455. 6d. until this week, when it has dropped 29. 6d. a ton, and is now quoted 435. to 435. 6d, Glasgow warrants have run their usual course of fluctuation since we last wrote, but they are at the end ot the present week not much below what they were three weeks ago. Scotch makers' iron, on the contrary, shows declines varying from 6d. to 38. 6d. per ton.—irron. div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.

• PRESENTATION TO THE CONDUCTOR. The annual meeting of. the members of Runcorn Musical Society was held on Tuesday evening, in Bethesda Lecture Hall. There was a good attend- ance. and Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys was voted to the chair.—Mr. John Birkett, hon. secretary, gave a report stating that the season just closed was the second in the history of the society. There were now about 180 singing members, and the vice-presidents numbered 32. The doings of the society during the past winter were fresh in the memory of all. They gave three concerts, which were of a high- class character, and could not have been better car- ried out by any of the Runcorn societies in the past. If the members zould continue to work harmoniously together, till success of the society in the future was assured. (Applause.) He announced that he should resign the position of secretary because he had not the necessary time to devote to the office.—Mr. R. Pierpoint read the treasurer's report, which showed that the year was commenced with a balance of £l7 18s. 6d., and at the conclusion of theseason the balance was £ll Bs. 4d.—The Chairman moved the adoption of the report, and said it wasa matter of regret that they had lost slightly on the session, but they must not be disheartened by it, and he should be sorry if the Committee were discouraged from launching out Into legitimate cost. If the past season had proved anything, it had proved that with really good concerts, they might expect good audiences, and he urged them to maintain the standard of the past season.—Mr. Handley seconded the motion.—The report was adopted.—On the proposition of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. T. Clegg, Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., was re-elected president by acclammation. The vice-presidents were re-elected en bloc, and the Committee were given power to add to their number. The following officers were also appointed : Hon. Sec., Mr. R. Pierpoint •, orchestral sec., Mr. W. B. Kay; treasurer, Mr. W. B. Frith; librarian, Mr. R. Moore; accompanist, Mrs. W. B. Kay ; conductor, Mr. E. Wynne-Humphreys auditors, Mr. H. Wright, and Mr. W. Jones; committee, Misses Simister, Jones, Eliza. Wright, Lizzie Crosby, and Nellie Handley ; Messrs. J. Littler, W. Crosby, T. Handley, R. Morris and J. Birkett. The Chairman commenced a discussion on the work for next season, and it appeared that it was intended to give three concerts, including the Messiah about Christ- mas and probably " Elijah " at a latter date. Before Mr. Humphreys vacated the chair, Mr. Littler advanced to the platform and said he had avery pleasant duty to perform. As a mark of their appreciation of his services as conductor to the Society for the past two years, the members had determined to make him a pre- sent and he had great pleasure in asking Miss Jones to hand Mr. Humphreys a martle'clock and a purse of gold (loud applause).—Miss Jones having made the presenta- tion, Mr. Humphreys said it had been said that it was more blessed to give than to receive. If that was true there were some of them having a very good time indeed that night. (Hear, hear and laughter) Because, if their pleasure and satisfaction exceeded his, it must be very deep and very hearty. His services had been rendered willingly, and inasmuch as they had seen fit to recognise them in this way, he could only assure them that he accepted the gift in the spirit in which it had been offered, namely most freely ay.' gratefully.. If it had not been fer the spirit of enthusiasm which had prevailed in the general bodyof the members, they could not have hoped to have done what they had. May that spirit continue! As long as it did continue and as long as there was an utter absence of sectarianism and clique- ism, which was the canker which ate away many such societies, he had no doubt of the future. (Applause.) To say that they had got hold of the masses of the people in Runcorn was very far from true. He should like to ask whether they as amateurs could not do something ; more to bring the divine gift of music within the reach of , those who at present it was practically beyond. There were many •organs in the town, one or two really fine instruments, why should these for all practical purposes , be boxed up except to grind out a few hymn tunes on a Sunday. He would venture to appeal to their organists,

ministers, leaders, trustees—whoever had charge of them —to see whether they could not do something to make these organs real instruments in the way of musical culture in the town. If they would throw open these organs he was prepared to db his partin getting amateurs and even professionals to come at nominal rates, and perhaps they would have the churches and chapels filled with audiences, who did not enter for any other pur- pose than an organ recital, and be ventured to think that they had gone in for a better purpose than keeping out altogether. (Hear, hear and applause.) In conelu-. sion Mr. .Humphreys again thanked those present for their gift. The timepiece, which is a very handsome one, was of black marble, and bore the following inscription : —" Presented to E. Wynne Humphreys Esq., by the ' members of the Runcorn Musical Society in recas nition of his services as conductor, 13th May, 1890." After a short Colicert, the room was cleared for dancing, which was continued until about three o'clock. Refreshments were provided.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the TJwn. Hall on -Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs E. Care D. Wright, B. Brown, J. Midwood, E. Cook, H. Timmis, Neil, W. J. Har- greaves, F. Heyes, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, S. Sadler, Dr. O'Keeffe, J. T. Allen (clerk), Carr (engineer), Sinclair (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspec- tor).

div.head: PanTRAIT OF THE LATE .ITR: HENRY DEACON.
div.p: PanTRAIT OF THE LATE .ITR: HENRY DEACON.

The Chairman read the following letter :—" Appleton ' House, Widnes, May 10M, 1890. Dear Mr. Gossage, I beg to offer through you, to the Local Board, a copy made by my son Allan of my husband's portrait by W. W., °Mess, H. A. I hope the Board will accept the , portrait, and I shall always be glad to think that it is hanging in the Boardroom with that of his ojd friend, your father. With kind regards, I am, dear Mr. Gossag,e, very sincerely yours, Caroline Deacon."— The Chairman said it gave him the greatest pleasure per- sonally to thank Mrs. Deacon for so kind a letter. It was also h:s pleasant duty to ask the members to accept the gift, and to convey their thanks to Mrs. Deacon and her son. The late Mr. Deacon had very strong artistic taste, aid thatpicture showed that his son was develop- ing that trait in a very able manner ; the Board wished him every success in the.artistic work he had under- taken. He proposed that the Clerk be instructed to write to Mrs. Deacon a cordial letter of thanks, accept- ing the gift, and also to thank Mr. Deacon for his work. (4,p'auee.) Mr. E. Corey seconded the motion, whikk was carried unanimously.

THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-PCOPOSED COLLECTIONS FOR

div.head: HOSPITALS.
div.p: THE HOSPITALS.

The Medical Officer reported to the Health Committee that during April there wete 103 births and 55 deaths, being at the respective rates of 39-87 and 21.2 per 1,000. Zymotic diseases caused one death. 37 cases of infectious disease had been notified. During the month there had been 15 patients in the Fever Hospital ; nine had been discharged, and six remained. It was recommended that the clergy of all denominations and the owners of the various works in the township be asked to co-oper- ate in establishing a Saturday• and Sunday collection towards the maintenance of the patients in the hospitals. —Mr. Wright, in moving the adoption of the minutes, referred to the proposes collection for the hospitals, and said he was confident the Committee's suggestion would be liberally responded to.—Mr. Carey seconded the motion, and the minutes were passed.

div.head: AN INCREASED RATE.
div.p: AN INCREASED RATE.

The Finance Committee reported that the estimated expenditure for the ensuing twelve months was as fol- lows :—Highway Committee, p 5,268 ; Health Com- mittee, £2,483; Finance Committee, £6,039 : total £13,790 ; add balance to debit of rates account £230 ss. ; total £14,020 Sc.; estimated receipts from increased assessments of works, &c., this year, £500; total amount required £13,520 ss. The actual expenditure during the past year was £13,110 3s. 7d. It was recommended that a general district rate of 2s. 6d. per £ with the usual deductions for land, railways &c., be laid for the year 1890-91, payable by two instalments—the first on date of demand and the other on 30th September next, estim- ated to produce £13,290, leaving a deficiency of £230 ss. Accounts amounting to £2,694 were recommended for payment.—Mr. Mldwood moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Brown drew attention to the increase in the estimates of the various Committees during the past few years. and said there were many professions of economy outside, but these appeared to be forgotten in the Boardroom. He could not vote for a half-crown rate, be- causd he believed that the, work could be done at a cheaper rate —Mr. Midwood said the increase in the estimate of the Finance Committee was brought about by providing sinking fund and interest for the various properties, &c., that had been erected by the Board. The expenses of the Fever alopital were great. It had cost £717 10s. to keep that institution for the past year, independent of the sinking fund.—The minutes were passed. THE FIRE BRIGADE. _ .
- _ It was resolved to invite tenders for the construction of 14 houses and fire engine station. This concluded the meeting.
:RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

- - _ The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery, on Wednesday. Mr. R. Morris presided and their were present the Rev. Dr. Gistaldi, Messrs. S Taylor, W. Littler, W. Mellor, and W. F. Salkeld (clerk.) INTERESTING STATISTICS.. The Secretary reported that the interments for 12 months to March 25th, were 408, corresponding period last year 400, increase 8. The fees received this year £377 175., last year £348 12s. 4d., increase £29 4s. Bd. The total number of interments since the opening of the cemetery March Ist. 1860 was 8572, classified as follows: Church 3,482, Dissent 4,406, Roman Catholic 684. The interments for the month of April numbered 41 • corres- ponding period last year 28 • increase 13. The fees received during the same period amounted to £36 75.; last year £37 13s. 6d. ; decrease £1 6s. 6d. FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended that notice be given to the overseers to contribute £6O to sinking fund account. Accounts amounting to £l5 19s. 7d. were passed for payment. It was reported that the consols in hand amounted to £552. It was recommended to pay off a mortgage of £3OO to the Lily of the Valley Lodge of Oddfellows.—The minutes were adopted. CATHOLICS AND THEIR DEAD. Dr. Gastaldi said he noticed that 684 Catholics had died and been buried in that Cemetery, and the order of service they performed was done in the open air, to matter whether it was a fine resplendent day, or a dark, gloomy, tempestuous day. Did not the Board consider that the Catholics as ratepayers had not a right to have a proper place where they could perform part of the service same as others. He did not desire to put the ratepayers to the expense of building a church for them, but had they not the right to take the bodies into one of the churches.—Mr. Taylor asked if the Catholics had a legal right to use the chapel in the Cemetery. If they had, he should support Dr. Gastaldi, because he considered Catholic ratepayers were equal to other ratepayers. If they had not a legal right they had a moral right to use the chapel. He supposed they could not usethechurchincon- sequence of being the Established Church,and he thought the sooner that law was altered ' and• the better.—The Chairman said Mr. Salkeld had made inquiries and found that at Warrington, Crewe, and Macclesfield, there were three chapels, one for each denomination. At Leek and Middlewich there were two churches only provided, and the Catholics could use the Nonconformist place, but no crucifix was to be placed there.—Dr. Gastaldi: Incase we , use the Dissenters' Chapel, shall we use it as a right and , not as a privilege.—The Chairman: Certainly—The Secretary said when the cemetery was made it was thought that two chapels would be sufficient for th,

town, and that if the Catholics applied for the use of the pissenters' Chapel there could be no earthly reason for preventing them. No application had been made until the present time, and he was of opinion that they had a perfect right to use it. He pointed out that the lunral arrangements should be made so as not to clash witn the Nonconformists.—Dr. Gastaldi then made the applica- tion required, and permission to use the Nonconformist Chapel was granted.

CHEMICAL LABOURERS' UNION. A well-attended meeting of the members of the Chemical Labourers' Union was held in the old toachhouse in Cotham-et, opposite the Town Hall, on Sunday afternoon. Mr. P. J. King, the organiser, gave a lengthy address in the course of which he said they had met to consider whether the organi- . . cation might not be cousidembly strengthened in St. [Helens. They had succeeded in gaining 2,900 members in St. Helens and Widnes, but he did not mean to stay his efforts until he had made the Union a still greater success. He urged that on and after the first of June all members of the Union must refuse to work with a black- leg. That, he said, was an important announcement to make and it might be fruitful of results not pleas- ing both to masters and to men. But it was neces- sary they should solidify their Union in order to be able to resist any encroachments that might be made on the just rights and privileges of the men connected with , the Union. He asserted that it would not be necessary to have a strike, but if,they followed his leadership they would accomplish their ends without sacrificing anything. He reqtrred to the strike of the salt cake men at the Wid- nes alkali works, and said he thought the action of the manager of the works was taken for the purpose of in- juring the organisation.--Mr. Richard Costello, one of Widnes chemical workers, gave a brief address, and said he hoped the St. Helens men would give them their hearty support during the dispute. Mr. Hodgson (St. Helens), expressed a hope that the struggle would be a success for the men.—After some further observations a resolution was unanimously passed "That this meeting of chemical workers of St. Helens, pledges itself toren- derthe Widnes men whatever assistance the Committee may consider them deserving otY

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Reynolds. ILLEGAL REMOVAL or. a Cow.—Wm. Worrell, a youth, was summoned for removing a cow, into an infected area under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act. Ralph Tickle, butcher, Sutton Weaver, was summoned for causing the cow to be removed.—Tickle said he pur- chased the cow in Warrington and it would have been slaughtered there had he not discovered that the animal was in calf. He had a veterinary surgeon's certificate, but not a license.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s. and costs. ASSAIILT.—Wm. Robertr,a boatman,was summoned for assaulting Mary Williamson,of Wellington-st., on the 3rd. May. There was a cross summons charging Williamson with assaulting Roberts.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys appeared for Williamson. It was alleged that Roberts went up to the woman and asked her what she knew bad about him. He then made use of vile language. and struck her with his fist. He atterapted to strike her again, but she put up her hand to protect herself, and it came in contact with his face.—On the other hand, it was alleged that the woman made use of most insulting epithets, and that she struck him in the mouth with her fist and kicked him. He then retaliated.—The Bench considered it a case of "six of one and a half-a-dozen of the other" and dithnissed bsth summonses.—James Yar- row and Elizabeth Ellen 'Wood, boat people, were sum- moned for assaulting another boatwoman named Matilda Shaw, on the 17th April.—The Bench dismissed the summons for the reason given in the last case. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence a fine of 103. and costs was imposed on each of the following : John Percival, Richard Pritchard, John Potter, Thomas Kelly, and Geprge Davies, James McTurk. Joseph Evans, John Jones, Thomas Comisky were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk. VAGRANTS.—Robert Porter, who said he was a collier out of work, was fined 6d. and costs for begging inHigh- st., or go to gaol for seven days. He went to gaol. John Watson, a navvy, was sentenced to seven days hard labour for begging in Bull's Head Hotel, Halton-road, on Saturday night.

SLEEPING OUT.—James McCormack, no settled resi- dence, a youth who had been 18 times before the court, was sentenced to seven days hard labour for sleeping in the Saf-ammoniac Works on the previous night. MESDAY.—Before Mr. H. %lade Deacon. DRUNK.—Michael Hiagins, Sutton's-lane, and Ann Tansy, Victoria-st., were each fined ss. and costs' for being drunk. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkincton.
DRUNK.—Patrick Miskell, Appleton, Cheshire, was fined ss. and costs for this offence.

div.head: THING H KARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORILESPONDRNT.
div.p: THING H KARD AND SEEN AT RUN- CORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORILESPONDRNT.

The Widnes Brine Scheme has fallen through, and the Widnes manufacturers will continue to pay the high prices demanded by the Salt Union. The news, of the failure to obtain Parliamentary sanction was received with great regret throughout the town; but it was felt that those who had the mattbr in in hand were not the people to be discouraged by one repulse, and that probably another Bill would benrn'd next session, and with b,tter success. It i:surori,.ng that a Hospital Sit today and a Hospital Sunday has not been established in Widnes before the present time, considering the great benefits derived from the Accident Hospital for many years, and the great boon the Infectious Diseases Hospital has proved in preventing the spread ot disease during its short existence. Both institutions were erected at the cost of the rate- payers, and are maintained out of the rates, although there are private benefactions, small in amount perhaps, constantly flowing in. Patients are charged for their accommodation, &c., at each hospital, but in the great majority of cases they are so poor and made poorer by their disease, that it is impossible for them to pay. There is a small charity fund which renders a little aid in such cases, but by no means equal to the demands made upon it, and it is to be hoped that the appeal of the Health Committee,for a collection at the works and the places of worship once a year. will meet with a ready and generous response from those in authority. The General District Rate at Widnes is year by year becoming heavier, and for the next twelve months will be half-a-crown in the .C, or an increase of 2d. in the .C. From the figures submitted at the last meeting of the Board it is doubtful if this will realise a sufficient sum to carry on the multifarious operations in the township and it will not be sur- prising if there is a deficiency at the end of the year, which will have to be made up afterwards. However, with new public offices, hospitals, night- soil depat, fire brigade station, road improvements, and a host of other things, a higher rate must be expected. The ratepayers cannot have the cake and eat it too. The sensation of the week in Runcorn has been the County Council inquiry into police administra- tion in Cheshire, and every tongue has been a-wag- ging qf ex-Inspector O'Donnell's impeachment of the Runcorn section of the force. The revelations he ha made are certainly of a startling character, but one tale is always good until another is told, and the public, if they are wise, will suspend their judgment until both sides have been heard. The annual meeting of Runcorn Musical Society on Tuesday. provided an interesting incident in the presentation of a handsome marble clock and a. purse of gold to the conductor, Mr. E. Wynne Hiimphreys, who is an admitted prinoe amongst the amateur conductors and who by his ability and enthusiasm has elevated our lccal Musical Society to a high position amongst such societies. In ac- knowledging the gift, Mr. 13 nmphreys made a speech which will well repay perusal, and it is to be hoped will bear wholesome fruit in the future.

TRAM-CAR ACCIDENT. —A serious accident which should act as a warning to mischievous lads occurred at Black- brook on Wednesday. A number of lads took the brake off a car belonging to the St. Helens Tramways Oorn- pans, which stood unhorsed at Blackbrook, and pushed it up the incline. They then got in, and as it as run- ning back a little boy named Fred Cunliffe was knocked down, and had his right thigh badly fractured. Dr. Hynes, St. Helens, and Dr. Hayward, of Haydock, were promptly in attendance. The boy was removed to the Haydock Cottage Hospital, and on Thursday he was in a critical condition. The car in question is run once a day, pending a settlement of the dispute, to show, the right of the company to the roads in Haydock.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A " LARK " WITH SERIOUS CONSEQUENCES.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, a 'bus driver named Richard Shaw, was charged with having stolen a razor, value 2s. 6d., from the shop of Gregory Murphy, barber, Scotland-road, on the previous day. Be admitted taking the razor, but said it was only done in fun; it was a lark. Defendant received an excellent character from his employer, and in consideration of that the magistrates directed that he be discharged on paying 'the costs of the prosecution, 20s. The money was paid.

div.head: UNDER THE SEAT._
div.p: UNDER THE SEAT._

John William Miller, a youth, was-brought before the Warrington magistratts on Thursday, on a charge of having travelled from Manchester to Liverpool, on the Cheshire Lines railway, without having previously pur- chased a ticket. When the train stopped at Warrington prisoner was found hiding under a seat of one of the carriages. He had neither ticket nor money, and said that he wanted to get to Liverpool. He was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 lays' imprisonment, with hard labour.

div.head: YOUNG MAIIKET THIEF.
div.p: A YOUNG MAIIKET THIEF.

John Griffin (a). son of Maria Griffin, now of Earles- town, but late of Silver-square, Warrington, was before the Warrington magistrates on Thursday on a charge of having stolen a pinafore nom a stall in the Market,on the previous day. He pleaded not guilty, but two com- panions established the charge against him. The Chief Constable said prisoner had been sent to goal twice, and 'birched three times, but as he suffered from an infirmity• he could not be sent to a reformatory. He was ordered to be imprisoned for seven days. ASSAI7LTS ON WARRINGTON POLICEMEN. '

John McDonald was brought up at the Borough Court, on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, and with assault- ing Constable Phillips. The officer was on duty in Buttermarket-st. when his attention was drawn to defen- dant, who was drunk and disorderly and making use of bad language. When the constable spoke to him the de- fendant struck him several times, and afterwards lay On the ground and began to kick. McDonald was com- mitted to prison for 14 days, with hard labour.—Mary Jane Oates was charged vvich being drunk in Winwick-st. ,on Saturday night, and with assaulting Constables Hol- lingsworth and Phillips. She was creating a disturbance, and the officers went to her, when she threw her child, only a few months old, on the footpath. It was picked up by her sister. She kicked and struck the officers. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.

DANGEROUS ASSAULT WITH A POKER. At the Warrington Police Court,on Monday, P. Walsh, a labourer, living in Ship-yard, was charged tvith com- mitting a violent assault on his mother-in-law, Ellen Higgins, by striking her with a poker on Saturday night. Constable Turner said that shortly after ten o'clock on Saturday night he and P.C. Bell were called to a dis- turbance in Ship-yard caused by the prisoner. They found the complainant bleeding from a wound on her temple. A few minutes afterwards Walsh ran out of the house with a poker in his hand, and shouted 66 I will do for some of you yet." Witness caught hold of him, and defendant threw the poker into the house. The defendant used bad language towards Mrs. Higgins, whose wound was subsequently dressed at the Infirmary. Complainant, who was not a willing witness, would not swear positively who struck her, but she admitted that there was no one but the prisoner to strike the blow. Walsh, who it was stated was usually a steady man, was committed to gaol for a month.

div.head: BATCH OP LODOING-HOUSE KEEPERS FINED.
div.p: A BATCH OP LODOING-HOUSE KEEPERS FINED.

At the Warrington. Borough Court, on Monday, several lodging-house keeper were fined for the offences specified below. The evidence was given by Inspectors Norman and Church.—Andrew Gleamond, 14, Ashton-st., was summoned for keeping more *persons in ,his house than, it was registered for, also for neglecting to have the ceiling and walls whitewashed. Inspector Church visited the house, and found eleven persons in it, al- though it was only registered for seven. It was in a very dirty condition. Afine of ss. and costs in each case, amounting to 365. altogether, was inflicted.—William Preston, 4, Hill-street, was summoned for keeping lod- gers without having his house registered. When Inspector Church visited the house he found 20 lodgers in it. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposecl.—Patvick Millett, 4, Ashton-st.. was similarly charged. There were seven persons in the house, four of whom were lodgers. Fined ss. and costs.—Robert Lomax, 2, Ashton-st., was then charged. There were eleven persons in the house, four being lodgers. It was only adapted for six. Fined ss. and costs—A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted upon Ralph Orton, of 10, Ashton-st., for a similar offence. There were eleven persons in the house—nine of a family, and two ledgers.

div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess, Councillor Voisey, and Mr. R. Garnett.

MISCELLANEOLIS.—Mary Matthews (51), was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour, for refusing to perform the task of work set her at the Workhouse and for wilfully breaking six panes cf glass. Susan Gibbon (34), charged with being drunk on Arpley Bridge, on the previous night, was sent to prison for a similar period. MONDAt.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Alderman Harrison, Alderman Davies, and Alderman
Sutton.

DRITHRENNESS.—John Macdonald, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st.' on Saturday night,l4 days; Michael Birmingham, drunk and disorderly at Bridge Foot, on Saturday night, ss. and costs; James O'Brien drunk and disorderly on Sunday night, ss. and Costs; Patrick Murray, drunk and disorderly, Percival's-fold, Ist May, ss. including costs ; William Gough, drunk and disorderly in Buckley-st., 4th May, ss. and costs ; and Thomas Kncckton, drunk and disorderly, in Scotland-road, May 6th, ss. and costs. BREACH or THE PEACE. —Two young men, named Lamb and Widdowes, were charged with fighting in Buttermarket-St., on the 3rd May. The case against Widdowes was discharged, and Lamb was bound over to keep the peace for six months. TVESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. E. M. Crosfield.

A WOMEN'S QUARREL.—Mary Jane Owen was charged with having assaulted Catherine Bate on Saturday night. The complainant, whose eyes were blackened, gave long statement to the effect that words took place in re- gard to "pegging some clothes," and that defendant struck her on the face with a portion of a lamp. The magistrates, after hearing evidence, said that the state- ments made were so conflicting, that theyhad no alterna- tive but to dismiss the case. DRUNKENNESS.—Dennis Sullivan, charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Mersey-st., on the night previous, was dismissed on payment of costs, 3s. 6d. Thomas Armstrong, for having been Jrunk in Bridge-st., on the previous day, was also ordered to pay ccsts, 35.6 d.

--- SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, appeared on behalf of the School Attendance Committee to prosecute a number of parents for neglecting to send their children regularly to school. One boy was ordered to be birched, and the usual fines were imposed in the other cases. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Mr. John Fairclough. DntsixErnvEss.—James Ward for having been drunk in Arpley, on the same morning, was fined ss. including Costs. SLEEPING Our.—William Owen, John Walsh, and George Little were each sent to prison for seven days for sleeping out at Arpley. ALLEGED THEFT OF A WATCH.—Catherine Taylor, was czarged with stealing a watch, the property of some person unknown, and Thomas Miskell was charged with having received it knowing it to have been stolen. Prisoners were apprehended at Salford whilst endeavour- ing tc pledge the watch, and were broughtto Warrington ' from Salford, by Constable Monaghan. Evidence of arrest having teen given, the prisoners were remanded.

WARRINGTON V. BOLTON. —Notwithstanding the dull weather, a great many people visited the Arpley ground on Saturday afternoon. Warrington won the toss, and started batting with S. M. and J. J. Crosfield, to the deliveries of Ellis and Chadwick. Off the last ball of the latter's first over, the Warrington captain was smartly caught by 0. P. Lancashire (1 for 6). :Wagstaff came next, but, with only one run added, retired without scoring, having been smartly stumped (2 for 7). R.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 17, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 17, 1890

Smith now joined J. J. Crosfleld, but they were only to- gether for one over, when the latter was clean bowled by Ellis (3 for 10). Clarke, Armstrong, and Podmore all retired without scoring, and six wickets were down for 16 runs. T. Jolley, on becoming Smith's partner, soon got to work. Both batsmen hit out hard and freely, and at 43 Tristram took the ball from Chadwick, but with no result, for in his first over Smith drove him twice to the boundary for 4. With the total at 60 for seven wickets, R. Smith was splendidly caught by Stan- ley,after playing a careful innings for 31,made up of two 4's, one 3, and five 2's. He was at the wicket 45 minutes, and assisted in putting on 53 runs. L. A. Voisey joined Jolley. The spectators were now treated to some good batting. Both men hit out freely, and brought on several changes of bowling, and it Was not until they had added 58 runs that a separation took place: Jolley, who re- tired with 49 runs to his credit, was well and deservedly applauded. His 49 took 55 minutes to compile, and included five 4's, two 3's, and seven 2's. Voisey was next out at 124, having been at the wicket for 35 minutes, putting 32 to his credit—two 4's, three 3's, and three 2's. The innings closed at five minutes to four for 124 runs. It is impossible to speak too highly of the batting of Smith, Jolley, and Voisey. Their hitting was hard and clean, and, as far as could be seen, neither gave the Bolton men a chance that was declined. The Bolton fielding was very good and close. At 4.20, 0. P. Lancashire and H. Clegg commenced their innings, to the deliveries of J. J. Crosfied and Captain Adams. Runs came freely from both men, and with the total at 28, Tolley took the ball from Crosfield, and the game got very slow from this point, neither batsmen being able to get the ball away. At 52, Smith replaced Adams. and in his second over, 0. P. Lancashire was easily caught by Wagstaffe. A. E, Stanley was very cleverly caught behind the wicket without scoring_ Rain came en then, and stopped further play. Full score

WARRINGTON T. BOLTON (2ND, ELEVENS).-111iS match was played at Bolton, on Saturday. The visiting cap- tain having won the toss, he and Dunbobbin went in to bat, the latter, unfortunately, being caught at point with the second ball. Brown came in and scored 6 be- fore he was dismissed by a good ball from Calderbank. Muir's stay was very short, but Bell made a stand, and rattled up the score quickly. After compiling 18 he was cleverly caught by Staton. Jefferson followed, and im- mediately commenced to hit out in a pretty easy style, he and Adamson carrying the score from 37 to past the century before he was run out. Unsworth knocked up 12, and rain intervening, play was brought to a close, much to the disappointment of both teams. Adamson played grandly for his score of 56 (not out), and on his retirement to the pavilion was accorded a hearty recep- tion. Score : '

div.p: NOTES ON E-2._HES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

After the performance last week against Lord Sheffield's team, the critics are coming to the conclusion that the Australian team is much stronger than some people imagined, and that with Murdoch in form they will not be easily got rid of by any team. The veteran's batting in the first fir V-class match he has played for five years was sornethint marvellous. It was another instance of a good man seldom losing his form. •

The accounts of Pilling's health are very unfavour- able. A few weeks past a statement appeared in print that he had nearly recovered from the sericus illness which prostrated him during the winter, and that he hoped to play regularly for his county during the season. This report was far more sanguine than the facts war- ranted, and now we hear that since he has been at Southport the great wicket-keeper has had a relapse, and there is really no chance of seeing him in the cricket field this summer. To the Lancashire eleven the loss of his services is a very serious matter, and will seriously handicap the bowlers.

div.head: FOOTBALL -RUGBY.
div.p: FOOTBALL -RUGBY.

Yorkshire is the county, for big football club balances. The treasurer of the Hull F.C. can boast of having £1.292 ss. 3d. in hand, although on the season's workings there has been a loss of £7O 18s. 6cl.—the result, chiefly, of wet weather in home matches.

Some interesting facts are also out respecting the Yorkshire Football Committee's financial year. Besides giving £2,000 away to the charities, the committee have a balance in hand of £l7l 17s. 2d., which is considerably more than the amount usually retained as a" back set.' The two semi-final Cup ties yielded a gross gate of £1.104 2s. 3d., whilst the total receipts at the final were £el9 19s. 7d. These figures are very much in excess of the amounts previously tako in the similar stages of the Yorkshire Cup competitik.

The Wigan fifteen during the past season have scored 38 goals and 68 tries, as against 15 goals and 21 tries. Out of forty-three matches played during the season Wigan lost exactly half-a-dozen,viz., Brighwise Rangers, St. Helens Recreation, Leeds St. John's, Cardiff, Peny- craig, and Leigh.

div.head: WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY BILL
div.p: WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY BILL
REJECTION OF THE SCHEME.
This Bill came again before a select committee of the House of Lords on Tuesday, Lord Basing in the chair.

Mr. Littler, Q.C.,.for the promoters,stated that he had a letter from Mr. John Garner, who was present, and who was a director of the. Winsford Town and Market Hall Company, and also' at director of the Winsford Gas Company, stating that he had had no notice whatever of any question affecting the scheme before the com- mittee. Mr. Garner asked to be informed by whose authority the seal of either company was attached to the petitions against the Bill. The 'promoters had indicated their willingness ts contribute to the local burdens beyond the ordinary rates., and, therefore, they would propose a clause which would impose a rate of ld. per 1,000 gallons of brine pumped, and this would produce £1,040 a year, or equal t 0,441. in the pound, towards the pool. rates.

, Mr. Balfour Browne then addressed the committee on ' behalf of the NorthwicluGhardians. He alleged that the scheme had been most hastily considered and ill-matured. The case for the Bill was • that Widnes would be ruined unless they were allowed to set up - the ammonia-soda. process. All he could say in answer to that was that up to the present time the trade of Widnes was not properly an alkali trade at all: 'The Le Blanc process must continue, because it produced not only alkali hut muriatic acid, which was-used as a bleaching powder, and also chlorate of potash The- real fact was that the bleaching-powder trade of Widneswas so prosperous that Widnes was prospering at the•expense of St. Helens and other places. rho Bill was really for the purpose of breaking up the Salt Union. The scheme was that of certain speculative gentlemen in Widnes, and could not serve any public purpose. Mr. William Gillett, general secretary of the Federa- tion of Saltworkers, examined by Mr. Lloyd, said the scheme would be like taking:the,b/ood out of theirbodies. It would thrcw a large number of men out of employ- ment. Since the formation of the Salt Union the work- men had had better remuneration and shorter hours.-- Cross-examined by Mr. Pembroke Stephens: Some salt works had been closed, and the work had to be divided. Mr. Thomas Ward, manager' of the Salt Union in Cheshire, examined by Mr. Lloyd, said that about 4,000 men were employed in the county in connection with the industry. Twenty or 30 men would be sufficient to do the whole of the pumping of brine in the district. About one-third of the men employed in the industry were engaged in the work of converting the brine into salt. Two men would be sufficient to work the pumping of 120,000 gallons of brine a day for Widnes. He was prepared with figures to show that, leaving out rent and office expenses, they could not make salt 'for less than 4s. mid. per ton in 1889. Since then the price of coal had advanced considerably, and now it was utterly im- possible to make salt at all under ss. ed. per ton. Mr. John Weston was of opinion that the scheme would seriously injure the salt indtarry of Cheshire. By the Chairman.—The proposed tax of a penny per ton of salt had nothing to do with the poor-rates.—Mr. Thomas Rigby, secretary of the Cheshire Agricultural Society, gave evidence to the effect that the local markets in Cheshire would suffer by the scheme,because a large por- tion of the trade would be removed. _ _

Professor Boyd Dawkins stated that the proposed new shaft would increase the tendbney to subsidence. The fall of the salt rock was in the direction of Mr. Timper- ley's farm. Mr. Clifford, addressing the, committee for some local landowners, contended that the promoters were bound to pay for wayleaves. Mr. Noble, for the Ship Canal Company, said they op- posed the scheme because it was a private speculation, and because the engineering part of the Bill was very de- fective.

Mr. M`Tear, manufacturing chemist, called on behalf' of the local Sanitary Authority, said that in his opinion, the ammonia-soda process would not seriously affect the trade of Widnes. He admitted that the profit on the pro- duction of hhlorate of potash isasjust enough to save the trade from ruin.

Mr. G. E. Davies, forme/Ty Government inspector of alkali works, agreed with the evidence of the last wit- ness. There had been no substantial diminution, of manufacture under the Le Blanc process at Widnes. The new process would simply add to the trade of the place. Mr. Gandy, land agent,. of Northwich, stated• his, opinion that the salt works.could be properly eatablished, on Mr. Timperley's farm. The land was within 50 yards. of the Cheshire Linesaailway. Mr. Fletcher, clerk to the Northwich Guardians was also called for the oppositiow. . .

Mr. Pembroke Stephens replying on the whole cased. said that if their lordship;did not pass the Bill it would be a declaration against the salt monopoly, and a,rejpe— Lion of the scheme would be a rejection of the principle of compensation for subsidence.
The bommittee, after a quarter of an hours's deliber- ation, decided that that the preamble of the Bill had been proved. The scheme is, therefore, lost for the session.

The sawing and planing mill _belonging toMessrs. Robey and Co., engineers, Lincoln, was burned down on Tuesday night. The loss is estimated at £lo,oooi. At Leeds Assizes on Tuesday William Whittiestony. aged 88, labourer, was sentenced to eight years' penal servi- tude for the manslaughter of his wife at Crigglestone. During a quarrel he so seriously injured the woman that she died. Bishop Westcott was formay enthroned in Durham Cathedral on Thursday. There was agreat gathering on the occasion, and the Bishop at the close of the service delivered an eloquent discourse, in which he touched upon the social problems of the day. The Ince Local Board, at its meeting on:Wednesday, passed a resolution protesting strongly against Baron Huddleston's description of she district colliers as" men almost approaching the condition of wild, beasts." It was also resolved to ask Colonel Blundell to bring the matter before the Home Secretary. . Nine thousand mine; s in the Hi! bao distnict struck work on Wednesday for better wages and shorter hours. A Berlin telegram of yesterday, with reference to the gasworkers' strike in that town, .states that although the gas supply was resumed on Tuesday evening, serious conficts continue between the police anclthe mob. Alfred Carter, a young man living. at Nelson, was be- fore the Bucks magistrates on Wednesdav , on the charge of being a wandering lunatic, and was handed overt to. the custody of his father. It appeared that the defen- dant had written letters to the Queen at Windsor Castle asking for money and proposing marriage to her Majesty.

THE BISHOP OF PETERBOROUGH ON CHURCH
SEATS.

Sir,—The Bishop of Peterborough recently said : "As regards seats in. church, I am glad te feel that those old inaccessible forti3sses, called pews; are rapiely appearing from our midst. I trust that the selfish pew- dam system is over for ever; and we make it a condition, in the Peterborough diocese, of every new church we build, that it shall be absolutely free and open. Aul soine how or other, in spite of prophecies to the contrary, 'I never afterwards hear of any complaints whatever. So I suppose the Rector and his people manage to settle it between them somehow. One poor old man I heard of went into a church and asked for the "poor man's seat." "There is no poor man's seat here" was the reply. "Go where you please."—Yours, &c., R. S.

ROMAN CATHOLICISM. Sir,—Mr. Foulkes in his letter to you in last Saturday's " Examiner" thinks I must be very dull of comprehen- sion, because I have not been duly impressed with the quotations he has so plentifully scattered (in season and out of season) during the oast few years. It is awfully unfortunate, but lam afraid lam no more impressed now than I was before reading his last letter to you. If anything I am more than ever cons :need that the posi- tion he has taken up is untenable. Please notice one extract," Romanism, a thing impos- sible to defend '." if this is so, why is it that the religion (that has no dtfence) has not gone to the dogs, after all the fierce onslaughts it has had to fight against? Does the Roman Catholic Church in this neighbourhood look as if it was in a dying state? Or have the followers of of that church any reason to feel discouraged when they look around ? According to Mr. Foulkes' own showing, the Eaglish Church is in danger, by having in its midst what he terms "Tractarians," many of whom he says are "only Papists in disguise." This does not look very cheering or encouraging so far as Mr. Foulkes' pet theory 13 concerned. Then again he says "Tradition is not wanted, for it v.ill not bear scrutiny in many cases." Let him stick to this, and I for one will, " cease from troubling "in the future. After all, I cannot see the drift or reason of Mr. Foulkes' hostility to the Romish or any other church which differs from him; in some cases in small matters of detail only. Does he thinkthat the gates of heaven are closed against all " Romanists," " Tractarians," " Unitarians," and other deneminations not exactly following his v'ews ? I shall feel obliged if Mr. Foulkes will give a straiyht ans- wer to this, as thewhole argument rests on this point. If it will not trouble Mr. Foulkes too much, I should like him to leave out quotations in his reply, as I have not vet quite recovered from the effects of the last, and another dose might be fatal.—yours respectfully, RUNCORN REOTAIL Runcorn, 13th May, 1890.

THE RELIGIOUS CONTROVERSY. Sir,—l am reading, just now, with deep interest. in- deed, the religious controversy which is going on at present in the columns of the" Examiner," between Mr. Robert Foulkes and Mr. Thomas Williamson. I did in- tend remaining neutral on the subject, but, as a Roman Catholic, I could no longer stand by with folded arms, and see Mr. Williamson attacked by such overwhelming odds as appear arrayed against him in last Saturday's isSue Of your paper. Mr. Foulkes knows as much about "Roman Catholicism as my coachman,and, unfortunately, Edit, that gentleman never yet cracked a whip. A particular friend of mine, however, says that my statement against Mr. Foulkes is altogether incorrect, /or, to his mind it appears that Mr. Foulkes is a good Roman Catholic, because Mr. Williamson, having given I Correct interpretation of what the practice of Roman Catholics is, Mr. Foulkes, in the face of it, pretends to know our holy religion better than ourselves • consequ- ently, it is but logic to admit that he must be a more enlightened Catholic than I am, for instance, who have been brought up in the faith from infancy. In the near future, Mr. Editor, (I tell you in confidence) it is my in- tention to call together a representative Committee meet- ing of the Catholics of Runcorn and district, and at that meeting I propose to move the following resolution,which I have no doubt will be carried unanimously, viz. "That we, the Catholics of Runcorn and district, assembled in council, recognizing clearly that Mr. Robert Foulkes understands the Roman Catholic religion much better than we do, hereby agree to bestow upon him im- mediately the dignity of Pope Foulkes I. of Cheshire." There will be no difficulty in ~ppointing "Truth," "Dis- senter," and G. W. Hargreaves, as his Continental travellers or agents for facts, which, like a drunken man, have but very weak legs to carry them along. With respect to Mr. Foulkes and his reference to our adoration of images, allow me to tender a simple ex- planation, together with a logical comparison on the same. I have fallen in love, Mr. Editor, with a charm- ing young lady of prepossesing appeap.nce: Se lives a long way from here, but we correspond regularly. Oirily. yesterday she enclosed me her photograph. Upon receiv- ing the letter, I eszerly tore oven the envelope and abstracted the earte-de-risite. I passionately kissed it. Horror of horrors, the thought immediately occurred to me, is Mr. Foulkes about ? I lookecl around, and see- ing I was alone, I heaved a deep sigh of relief. Had Mr. Foulkes been about, unquestionably in this week's " Examiner" an expectant public would have been treated to a long letter, in which he would endeavour to gull them into believing that he actually saw a Papist adoring a picture of his future bride. My thoughts when kissing the preserved shadow flewwith more than lightening rapidity to the original ; and so it is with the pious Catholic, who, kneeling before a statue of Our Blessed Lady, forgets for the time his short visit on this material world of ours, and lets his thoughts soar to higher and holier things in the better world above. The Catholic Church has withstood in the past greater blows hurled at it than we can ever expect in the future from Mr. Foulkes, " Truth," " Dissenter" or G. W. Hargreaves. To-day she stands humble, yet in proud defiance of her enemies, pursuing the "even tenor of her way," just as she did centuries and centuries ago. The present calumnies raised against her now, by Mr. Robert Foulkes and Co., resemble "the puny cry of a barndoer fowl." Mr. Williamson's noble defence of her prinniples I compare to " the wild scream of America's eagle. I hsve no intention N quote Scripture in her defence, to be misinterpreted by men of the stamp of Mr. R. Foulkes and Co., whose opinions against her do not tell as much, in comparison, as a drop of water would if cast into the Mersey at high tide. In conclusion my advice to Mr. Williamson would be to withdraw at once from thopresent controversy,which, "like the airy fabric of a vision leaves not a wreck behind."

Convince a man against his will He's of the same opinion still: Apologising for trespassing so much on your valuable space,—l remain, Mr. Editor, yours very truly, .11ANG4TIR A. Runcorn, 13th May, 1890.

THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH. . Sir,—l am glad your correspondent "A Dissenter" does not wish to prolong the controvcrsy. It does not seem inviting anyway, seeing all the letters you publish this week on the subject. I have tried to give what I believe to be a tiustworthy, explanation of the Catholic doctrine concerning the "Mother of God," and having ,idone this, I feel have done my duty. If your cones- , pondent "A Dissenter" cannot make hisinind clear on ,these points I cannot help it. The questions in dispute between your correspondent and myself are, not whet individual Catholics may convey to the mind of the stranger, bat .what is the real teaching of the Catholic Church on the matter. There may, certainly, be some Catholics, who, when making use of loving expressions may seem to attribute to the Blessed Virgin more than I have stated here, but they are to be understood in a limited sense meant by Catholics themselves, that is in *ay consistent with Catholic teaching and spirit, and ret in the unlimited un-Cathelic sense which persons not understanding that teaching may be led to apply to the to. These tender expressions ought not to be ridged rpf by cold or hostile criticism, for they, spring from I.l:lt.tfelt devotion and unmeasured love. 1: it were permitted to take offence at expressions Ilich are only true in a limited sense, surely Christ can- i.ot be said to encourage the hating of fathers and uloLliers, &c., when He said, "If any man come to me and bate not his father, &e., Am, he shall not be my

disciple," St. Luke xiv., 26. Also the passage in St. Mathew v. 30, might be taken to justify self-mutilation, when it says, "If thy right hand scandalize thee, cut it off" If, therefore' even in the interpretation of Holy Scripture it would be a wrong principle to take, in the 'full extent, expressions that were meant to be under- stood in a qualified sense only ; so still more unjust it would be to apply this wrong principle to expressions tound in books of devotion, or in religious poetry in which a certain latitude to the expansion of a warm heart is allowed. I say that the Catholic Church does not teach her children to worship the Blessed Virgin, the saints, or angels, as I have explained before. In the • Established Church of England the bridegroom has to say in the marriage service "With my body I thee worship." Is that idolatry? Again, .for instance, mothers often call their children little "angels," "kings," and "queens," and are said to adore and idolize them, and no one ever thinks of blaming such tender exagge- rated expressions of heartfelt love. No one should object to such tender expressions, more especially when the speaker declares his meaning. In this also must Catholics be judged by their intentions as regards "Mary." Your correspondent is deceived when he supposes that Catholics substitute the Blessed Virgin or the saints for Christ. This is a very general and mistaken notion. Catholics do not ask grace from the Mother of God, nor the saints, nor angels; they merely ask the saints to pray. that God may grant them all necessary graces through Christ. They say,when addressing God—" Have mercy on us "' • but when addressing the Blessed Virgin or the saints "Pray for us." Catholics know well that the Blessed Virgin, or the saints, can give us nothing of themselves, but that all the virtues, merits and graces of the saints are derived not from themselves but from Jesus Christ. Catholics glorify Him in His mother, in His saints, and in His angels, and in the pictures and images of Him which they keep with respect and vener- ation. . The honour given to the Blessed Virgin, &c., is only meant to glorify Jesus who by His mercies and graces, has made these saints what they are, worthy of our veneration and imitation, and as often as Catholics show respect or veneration before a picture or image of Jesus, they uniformly refer both, not to the mere matter before them, but to the prototype Jesus Christ himself. If your correspondent reconciles this with his idea. of idolatry, then all I can say is that God may grant him the happiness of one day being able to see for himself in Heaven. In answer to the second paragraph concerning Mary being the mother of God, I have only to add that it has always been believed by Catholics that Mary was the mother of Jesus Christ, the eternal son of God, no other than the divine word made flesh, and that he had two natures and only one person,which is that of the son,the second person of the adorable 'Trinity. I am astonished how any Christian can call in question the divine maternity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, or doubt whether she is to be styled the mother of God. For, if our Lord Jesus Christ is God, and that he is so the Scriptures clearly teach, the Holy Virgin His mother who brought Him forth must consequently be the mother of God. Not that the divine word had a beginning from Mary, but that in her was formed a pure body animated with a rational mini to which the word was hypostatically united and so became man in one and the same divine , person. Thus, in the order of nature, a woman who lbears a son is truly called the mother of a man, although she only concurn in the formation of his body and has no I part in the creation of his soul. Re-examples. I wish to point out to yeur correspond- ent that what individuals may do or say is a different affair altogether from the teaching of the church. With regard to the reading of the Bible and tradition, I may mention that the passages your correspondent states are not at all favourable to his argument. Besides, he does not agree with the teaching of the church ; he has only the security of his own one judgment. The Catholics have that of the whole church. I prize the Bible as dearly as any of your numerous correspondents, and read it over and over and am not forbidden but encour- aged to do so. My friend, Mr. Editor, rejects tradition • now how in the name of fortune can he reconcile this idea with the ' knowledge that it is from tradition that we know which books are divine, and which are not? How does he know that the Bible is the Bible except by tradition? It is evident therefore in a matter of such awful import- ance as is the integrity of the Scripture, if he rejects tradition then he can have no certainty that he is right in anything. The church does not create new doctrines, but it de- fines passages of Scripture, and let me remind him that ' there are passages of Scripture which are not yet de- fined, and as they have never been disputed perhaps never shall. I certainly draw nice distinctions, which is one thing your correspondent admits, and shall not allow his ?pinions to pass without stating that his and mine are in entire disagreement as regards what Catholics believe and teach. And now. Mr. Editor, I must respectfully ask your cor- respondents to come one at a time, and just before I con- clude I think you might allow me a parting sentence to "Truth," viz, that I am more familiar with the teach- ing of my own church than he is any way, and ani thoroughly convinced after a thorough search ; and if I am wrong it ig no great harm done, if I submit my judg- ment to Rome. And one also to Mr. Foulkes, viz. :—Radically wrong again, and no attempt could touch it for errors ; and lastly I must not forget to enlighten Mr. Hargreaves— that, in the pastoral which he speaks of, the Pope con- demns the spreading broadcast of Bibles which are wrongly translated. I may appease his wonder even more so as he betrays a limited acquaintance with the meaning of the Catholic doctrine to point out that Papal infallibility means that the Pope cannot err when (a) speaking ex-officio I. e. as Pope he (b) defines some doc- trine (c) concerning faith or morals which (d) he declares must be held by the whole church (see Vatican Council Decrees.) For a Papal utterance to be infallible, all these conditions must be fulfilled. Hence a Pope laying down laws for his temporal subjects is not infallible ; a Pope speaking or writing or preaching as a private theologian is not infallible, even though his discourse be on faith and morals, and very strongly worded. Neither is he infallible in the government of his church, e. g. in suppressing monastries here and there, &c., at different times in different parts of the world. Having accomplished my object viz., that of denying these false statements, I now conclude, begging to be excused for occupying so much of your valuable space. —I remain, Mr. Editor, yours very truly, THOMAS WILLIAMSON.

div.head: SHIP CA.NAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CA.NAL.

• • SHIP CANAL CRICKET CLUB. • The Manchester Ship Canal (No. 6 district) Cricket Club played the first of their season's fixtures on their ground at Morrisbrook on Saturday afternoon, when thi.y obtained a creditable victory over their opponents, Grappenhall St. Wilfred's. Score :—Thelwall, 58 ; Grap. penhall, 32.

TEA AND MEETING. Yesterday week Mr. Davidson, of Grappenhall, gave a tea to some seventy of the mothers and friends in the schoolroom in connection with the Mission Hall at Morris Brook. Addresses were given by Mr. Davidson and Mr. G. Manning, and there were also songs and solos. At the close of the meeting, which is an annual affair, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Davidson fer his generosity. DISTINGUISHED VISITORS. On Saturday Sir Edward Watkin, M.P., visited the Manchester Ship Canal Works with a small party of friends who were staying with him at Northenden. The party included Mr. and Mrs. Yates Thompson, Mr. and Mrs. Henry Gladstone Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., Sir Benjamin Baker, le engineer of the Forth Bridge; Mr. W. Pollitt, of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway; Mr. Robert Perks and Mrs. Perks, and Mr. Leader Williams, C.E. The visitors were conducted over the works from Salford to Warrington by Mr. Leader Williams and contractors, and lunched with Mr. Walker's executors at the Saracen's Head. at Wilderspool. The proceedings were of a strictly private character, and the distingnished visitors only remained in the district about an hour. LECTURE BY MR. W. JOHNSON, C.E. On Monday evening, in connection with the annivers- ary of Bridge Foot Mission, a lecture on the Manchester Ship Canal waa given in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Bold- street, by Mr. 'William Johnson, C.E. The chair was taken by Mr. E. J. Guest, 8.A., J.P., and there was a , fair attendance. The lecturer dealt first with the history of the undertaking. Speaking of the voluntary rate which was laid in Manchester, Salford, and Warrington, he remarked that the Warrington people seemed rather inclined to have the money which their rate produced returned. (Hear, hear.) On the 11th November, 1887, Lord Egerton of 'ration cut the first sod of the canal at Eastham, Sir Joseph Lee cut the second, and Mr. Leader Williams, after cutting a third, wheeled the sods away and tipped them as spoil. The gigantic work so auspiciously begun had continued with unparalleled pro- gress up to the present time. The canal was 35 miles three furlongs in length. Its bottom width was 120 feet, and the top width 150. There would be five sets of locks—Eastham. Latchford, Irlam, Barton, and Mode Wheel. The lock gates.at Eastham would be the largest ever constructed.. Itnagine a door five storeys high, the width of the street, and weighing 250 tons. Near Tom Paine's bridge would be entrance to the Warrington dock, which would cover about 22 acres of water space. The dock would be connected with the London and North- Western 'Railway. The lecture was illustrated by maps find diagrams; and a number of capital views of the works, &c., were shown by means of an oxy-hydrogen lantern, which was manipulated by Mr. Harrison.—A vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer at the close.
