div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 17,1890.

tain a high-!evel vehicular bridge near-Latchford station and, it can only agree to a high-level vehicular bridge on condition that the Ackers-lane swing bridge is retained" With regard to the last clause of the re3olution, he said it was a literal copy of the proposition unanimously adopted a fortnight ago by the Daresbury Highway Board. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. HARTLEY seconded the amendment, and referred to the dangers of collisions of vehicles on a high-level bridge o2sft. width. Mr. Joao DARBYSHIRE, in supporting the amendment, said that at the meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board, at which the proposals of the Canal Company were accepted, there were 24 members present at the commencement, but ten„ of these had left before the division was taken. Of, the remaining 14 one ex-officio member abstained from voting, and nine voted for the proposal and four against. Of the nine who voted for the proposal six of them resided in remote townships, and several of them said after the meeting was over that they didn't know where the roads to be affected by the decision were, and that they were not interested in the matter: (Hear, hear, and laughter.) All of them were perhaps liable to vote to please their frionds,and five out of the nine did that, he believed. (Applause.) Alderman HARRISON thought the swing bridges would have to be much oftener open than Mr. Walker seemed to think. He also referred to the great advantage which the new roads being made by the Ship Canal Company would he to the localitv.• _ .

_ Mr. JOHN WHITE spoke in favour of Alderman Harri- son's proposal. He referred to the difficulties the Canal Company had had to meet, and said he had always found the Company's officials most courteous and wishful to do the utmost they could for the districts through which they were passing. He though, it would be a very serious thing for the residents on the other side of the Canal, if for the future they ,had to be at the mercy of the swing bridges. For all practical purposes the Canal would be the division between the counties of Lancashire and Cheshire, and a high-level bridge would be a permanent link between those two counties. If they rejected the proposal, they would regret it the longest day of their lives. (Hear, hear and applause.) ,The Rev. J. W. VARLET supported the amendment, and spoke strongly in favour of the retention of Ackers-lane swing bridge. The argument that few vehicles passed down Ackers-lane was no argument against the bridge, as they ought to look at what the traffic was likely to be in the future. (Hear, hear.) He could not, he said, understand why all the new roads were being made on the south side bf the canal rather than the north side. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. F. L. GOOD also supported the amendment, and dealt in particular with the hardship it would be upoq working-men, and people who could not afford to order out their carriage and pair, to have to climb the high-level bridge every time they wished to cress the canal. As to the traffic along Acker's-lane, he said there would, even at present, be much more than there was but for the gates at the railway level crossing. (Ap- plause.) The amendment proposed by Mr. Walker wasthen put to the meeting and carried, the numbers being declared by the Chairman as 38 for and 28 against. Mr. W. DAVIDSON next moved the following resolution "That a copy of the foregoing resolution -be sent to the Corporation of Warrington, the Cheshire County Council, the Daresbury Highway Board, and the Manchester Ship Canal Company, with an earnest request that these various bodies will act in accordance with the wishes of the inhabitants." Mr. GRIMSHANT seconded the proposal, which was agreed to only .Alderman Harrison holding up his hand against it. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meet- ing.

div.head: LATCEIFORD BRIDGES.
div.p: LATCEIFORD BRIDGES.
3IEETING OF RESIDENTS. On Thursday ey ming a largely-attended public meeting of the ratepayers and inhabitants of Latch- . .
ford. drappenhall,- and vicinity, was held in the Parish Room, .Latchford, "to _take into considera:

tion the decision of the baresbury Highway Board with regard to the proposed high-level vehicular bridge, and the abandonment of two swing bridges; and to pass resolutions thereon." The chair was taken by Major Litton, J.P., and there were also on the platform Messrs. J. Walker, J. Lee and 0. Brook (local engineer of the Ship Canal Company). Amongst the audience were the Revs. F. L. Good
and J. W. Varley, Alderman Harrison, Councillor Tinsley, Messrs. J. White, J.P., H. Milling, G. Dakin, J. Darbyshire, W. Davidson H. Woods, Wallington,

_ The CHAIRMAN, in explaining the objects of the meeting, referred to the various bridge schemes for crcssing the canal at Latchford, that had been discussed and suggested, and also to the action cf the Daresbury Highway Board in the matter, as previously reported in our columns. On Monday, he said, Mr. J. C. Parr, the chair- plan of the Daresbury Highway Board, called upon him, and said that they had got what he (Mr. Parr) considered very advantageous terms for that _district from the Canal Company, though he

could not exactly remember what tliey Were, bui pro- mised to do his best to get the plans 'did before that meeting that night. On Tuesday he received a note from Mr. Parr, saying that he had made arrangements with Mr. Brooke to meet them at Mr. John White's office, _ . _ .
or Wednesday morning, and he .(the Chairman) weni there and met Mr. Parr . and Mr. Brooke, the latter of

whom very kindly explained everything and produced plans in regard to the proposed alterations. Mr. Brooke had also very kindly come there.that evening to explain what course was recommended, and the course that had

been adopted by the Highway Board. The Chairman then referred to letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. J. C. Parr, Dr. Gornall, Mr. J. Winser, and Mr. Edward Greenell, junior. Mr. Edward Greens.lt
wrote that he hoped the meting would support the

ide-a--oflhaving a 'permanent bridge as suggested by the Daresbury Highway Board. Mr. J. Winser wrote "I hope the meeting will strongly urge the necessity of two swing-bridges being provided, one at Knuts- ford-road and the other at Ackees-lane ; also a high lever vehicular bridge at Common-lane for the rail- wac station and other purposes." Dr. Gornall wrote, "it seems to me there is a danger of the comfort and the convenience of the masses being sacrificed for that of the classes. The number who require a per- . . . . . . . .

manent high level vehicular bridge isinsignificant, NO-dist their wants would be well met by the terms offered by the Ship Canal Company through their engineer, Mr. Leader Williams, namely, a high level footbridge and two swing-bridges." Mr. 0. linooxe then,en theinvitation of the Chairman, displayed plans of the proposed scheme, and answered the questions put to him by those present. 'He prefaced his remarks by saying that Mr. Leader Williams regretted very much not having been able to show the plans to the residents of that district before this, but if they only knew the way in which the Ship Canal Company had been thrown about from pillar to post like a shuttlecock by the County Council, the railway company, and the Highetay Board, instead of blaming Mr. Williams they would pity him. They had had three sets of plans drawn out and presented, but it was only lately that they had been able to come to any terms. They had endeavoured to meet everyone's views —the County Council, the residents of the district, and the Highway Board. In the scheme of 1885, it was pro- posed to have swing bridges at Twenty-step Bridge, at Ackere-lane, at Grappenhall-road, and atKnutsford-road, but from the very first, after the plans were passed, it was clear that the Gmppenhall-road bridge and the Knutsford-road bridge must always be open at the same time,they were so near together. The Grappenhall-road bridge, so far as convenience to the public was concerned, was, therefore, a dead letter. The Dares- bury Highway Board were asked to allow the Grappenhall-road swing bridge to be done away with, and they said they would if they were given the quid pro quo of a foot-bridge over the canal near Common-lane. Then the Railway Company came upon the scene and wished, if possible, to have a high-level vehicular bridge, and the Canal Company were willing to give this on mndition of the abandonment of Ackers- lane swing bridge. Mr. Brooke also mentioned that he had had the vehicles which went along Ackers-lane counted, and he found that the greatest number in any one day was twelve, and six of these went and came, I being in fact bakers' and butchers' carts. The proposals as they now stood were as follows. It was proposed to straighten the Northwich-rd., between Wilderspool Brewery and Twenty-step Bridge, to make a new road along the south bank of the canal from the Northwich- , rd. to Ackers-lane, to abandon Ackers-lane swing bridge, and to make a high level vehicularbridge, with agradient of one in 25, over the canal from Common-lane. The swing bridge between Knutsford-road and Grappenhall- , read would still be made. I In answer to various questions put to him, Mr. 13eocem said the new Latchford station would be very much nearer Wash-lane than the present one. All the new roads and approaches to the high-level bridge would have public roads, and they would not depend on the goodwill of the railway company or canal company. In answer to Mr. Walker. Mr. Brooke said that the approach from Knutsford-road to the high-level bridge would, at the point of intersection, be six feet about tile level of Graprenhall-road, and consequently the fatter road would have to be raised to that extent. Mr. J. DARBYSHIRE said he supposed that if the ap- proaches were made to the high-level bridge it would not be pcssible to gat upon them at all except at the ends of the approaches. Mr. BROOKE, in reply, said he had no doubt that, if the inhabitants of Latchford desired it, steps might be made at the side of the approaches. In reply to the Rev. J. W. Varley, Mr. BROOKE said people coming from Latchford would get upon the approaches I to the bridge about opposite Dalby Villas/ Replying to Alderman Harrison, Mr. BROOKS said that the distance from Acker's-lane to Warrington bridge by way of the proposed new road and Wilderspool would only be about fifty-yards further than by way of Latchford. The Rev. F. L. Goos : At what hour of the day did you commence to count the vehicles passing along Ackere-lane, and at what hour did you close ?—Mr. Brook : Five in the morning till seven at night. A vote of thanks was then accorded Mr. Brooke for his explanation. Alderman HARRISON paid that perhaps the plans that had been laid before them were not all they could wish, and no doubt there would be some inconvenience, to which some people would be subjected, but whs there ever a great work originated and carried aut to a suc- cessful issue without inflicting inconvenience upon some- body? On the other hand the canal would be a.great convenience and in all probability a source of great pro- fit to the commercial interests of Lancashire. If that was the fact was it not most desirable not to throw any undue obstacle in the way of the Ship Canal Company and of their undertaking? (Hear, hear.) He did not hesitate, therefore, to support the plan proposed by Mr. Brooke, as the best they were likely to get. The Cafial Company had had great obstructions to deal with, but he hoped Latchford would not distinguish itself by any captious opposition, and he had pleasure inproposing that the plans submitted to them by Mr. Brooke be ap- proved. (Applause.) Councillor TINSLEY seconded the proposal, and said there was no doubt whatever in his mind that they ought to have a stationery bridge. Mr. Jogs WALKER thought there VW something,to be said on the other side. He thought they might put themselves in a better position than by adopting those plans, and, in fact,'he considered they were in a lietter position before the present plans were submitted. In the Act they .were entitled to three swing bridges at Latchford, and he submitted that if they had to go back to that position, as was suggested by Mr. Leader Williams a fortnight ago, they would be in a better position than they would be in that night by adopting the proposals submitted to them. (Hear. hear and applause.) Why were they to sacrifice Acker's-lone swing bridge, for that was really the crux of ihe whole question ? The Ship Canal Company were simply trying to get their scheme through as cheaply as they could ,and he had nothing to say against that; but on the other hand residents of that district had an equal right to pro- tect their own interests. (Hear, hear.) It was in the interest of the inhabitants of Latchford to be able to cress the canal at as many points as possible, and he submitted that it was best 'as in the first instance to have the three swing bridges, so that they could walk quietly over the canal without having to climb a sort of Pendia Hill. (Laughter) But if they were te make a little personal sacrifice,let them revert to the scheme by which they would have a high-level foot- bridge and retain Arkers-lane swing bridge. If they adopted the plans put before them that night, they would have no means of crossing the canal between Stockton Heath and the Knutsford - road swing bridge except the high-level bridge. They should remember that the town was grewing, and they ought to give it a chanee of growing in the Acker's-lane direction. (Hear, hear.) Having referred to the disadvantages of a high-level goods station at Latchford, Mr. Walker said that no doubt the railway company wanted the high-level vehicular bridge, but he did not think that 19-20ths of the people of that locality should be put to inconvenience to save the pockets of either the railway company or the Ship Canal Company. He contended that with the Canal Company it was simply a question of saving some thousands of pounds, and not one of public convenience. With re- gard to the delays that it was said would be occasioned by the swing bridges, he was of opinion that most people would not be delayed, on an average, more than once a week, and surely for the sake of avoiding this little obstruction they were not prepared to sacrifice two swing bridges in order to get one high-level bridge. Mr. Walker then proposed the following amendment That this meeting of the inhabitants of Latchford, Grappenhall, and vicinity is strongly of opinion that two swing bridges—one at Grappenhall-road, and one at Ackers-lane—ought not to be abandoned in order to oh-

div.head: SANITARY CONDITION OF WARRINGTON. By SANITAS."
div.p: THE SANITARY CONDITION OF WARRINGTON. By SANITAS."

The concise and vigorous report of the Medical Officer on the insanitary condition of certain parts of Wairington,should lead to some very speedy and marked improvements, or the burgesses of the town should peremptorily demand to know the reason why. These improvements should be especially insisted upon by that by no means small section of the townspeople who suffer from the evils alluded to. This section may, on the whole,be composed of comparatively poor, and, individually, not "influen- tial, people, but they have votes, which, if cast with some degree of unanimity, would tell a signi- ficant tale at a municipal election. To see how great is the need, and how ample is the score, for improvement, let us briefly quote a few of the Medical Officer's remarks. He tells us that, in the North-West Ward, in the neighbourhood of Lilford- st., Pierpoint-st., Catherine-st., and Hoyle-st., at the time of his visit some of the passages were in such a condition as nearly to be impassable. "In many cases the,pails were embedded in soil, so that in re- moving a full pail the contents would be spilt over; in fact, in numerous cases, the pail stood in a small cesspool of solid and liquid excreta. The yards in this district are, with very few exceptions, un- paved, and are, therefore, not kept clean, a clean yard being quite a novelty." In the neighbour- hood of Tanner's-lane there are back passages and yards "as insanitary as they possibly can be:' Coming to the North-East Ward, the next populous district of the town, we have, in some parts, back- to-back houses—houses with no through ventila- tion, and ." domestic darkness and general dirtiness of dwellings." In Haydock-at. the houses are old and di lapidat ed, andbadly kept in repair, the walls are gnie,rally damp, the mortar between the bricks perished, the surface of yards, most defective, pail closets imperfect, the grids of traps absent, and slop water soaking into the surface of the yards. The passages to the various courts had invariably that smell of. fustiness due to the deposit of ex- creta and other filth, and the difficulty of cleansing an unmade and imperfect surface. The passage between Silver-square and Oliver-st. in a most filthy condition; Silver-square and the streets in the Hardy-st. district still unmade; passages in the Crossley-&t. district in a terrible state, and in Back Crossley-st. an abundance of decomposing organic matter, which must, under favourable circum- stances, cause a pollution of the atmosphere. and thus lower the standard of health—such are some of the sanitary defectsof the town, which the aledieal Officer formulates after a personal inspection. It can hardly be denied by anybody that the re- port of thei Medical Officer reveals in some respects a state of things that is not at all creditable to the town. It is true, no doubt, that several of the evils he points out are more easily seen and exposed than. remedied. The local Sanitary Authority has not been endowed with boundless or absolute pow- ers even in things sanitary. The powers of the Committees of the Town Council, and of the Town Council itself are strictly limited and restricted by law, and outside those limits and restrictions the 1 Council cannot act. It may easily be believed, therefore, that in some directions the work of sani- tary improvonent has been altogether stopped by legal prohibition, and impeded in other instances by legal doubts and technicalities. But after mak- ing ample allowance for cases of this kind, there still remains in Warrington a very great deal to be done that should not for so long a time have been left undone. Take for example the long catalogue of unmade streets, back passages and yards. Why have these been left in the state they are for so long a time? There can be no question that the Corporation has had the power either to apply a remedy themselves or to compel others to apply it.. One is, therefore, almost forced to the conclu- sion, either that the Committee which has charge . of this department of Corporation work has been extremely c3reless and dilatory in fulfilling one of its most important and obvious duties, or that the private interests of owners of property, upon whose sboulders the cost of making these improve- tents 4114, have been allowed more weight than 'considerations of public good. It may be said that property owners have their 'rights as well as their responsieilities. That is a proposition which can- not be disputed. They have aright to their rents, , and that is a righti which is, as a rule, rigidly en- forced., And it s a right which is none the less rigidly enforced where the landlord has evaded such au elementary responsibility in all well-goy: trued communities as that of putting his tenants' houses and their surroundings in a decently habit- able condition. It should be remembered by those who champion the clams of landlords to draw rents from insanitary property, that the landlord, as a landlord, is not a philanthropist. In a general way a person who embarks on the business of a property owner does so for profit, and if we may judtze by the number of people who have an ambition that way the business is not found to be an unpre- fitable one.'While, therefore, fully admitting the . . riglit' of the landlord to his profits, it is surely.per- missible to say that he should never be allowed to subject other people to health-destroying influences, and, further, that the local authority which permits him to do so is failing to fulfil its primary duty. It is a thing to be regretted that better means than dry and abstiuse statistical tables do not exist, or are not used, for demon- strating the close and necessary connection between the sanitary condition of a community and the state of its general health. If you hold a lighted lamp near a thermometer you at once see the mercury rise in the tube; take it away and the mercury descends. The relations of cause .and effect are obvious and striking. The heat of the lamp is the cause which expands and raises the mercury, and immediately upon the taking away of

the heat the mercury; contracts and descends. Now, there is just as intimate a relationship between them- sanitary condition of houses and their surroundings and the death and sick rates amongst the inhabit- ants of those houses, as there is between heat and the expansion of mercury. The connection in the one case is not so obvious, it is not seen at a glance as in the other ease, but it is none the less inevitable. Other things equal, there must, in the very nature of things,be more deaths and more sickness amongst people who live in badly-built and badly-main- tained houses, and in the midst of unpaved yards and unmade streets and 12ack-lanes, from which, under certain circumstances unwholesome exhala- tions must arise', than there will be amongst people who are subjected to none of these, evil influences. Cofisidering these things, is it not the manifest duty of those in whose hands have been placed the power and responsibility to remove, without:the slightest delay, all preventible causes of death and , sickness? To go back for, a moment to the illustra- tion just used, suppose that some deplorable conse- quences resulted from placing or leaving a lamp near a thermometer. In such a case,would not those who permitted the tamp to,remain in such a posi- tion lay themselves open to a charge of extraordi- nary remissness or blameable carelessness, if even to no stronger charge? Yet this is a fair illustration of the action of a corporate body which permits to exist year after year. such causes of mortality and , sickness as, at all events, some of those pointed out , by the Medical Officer of Health,—causes which it ; has the full power, and which it is its bounden duty, to remove.

div.head: COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

A well-informed London correspondent says a report is current in political circles that if the Government relin- quish the licensing clauses in the Excise Duties Bill Mr. Goschen will resign, the scheme havingln a special sense originated with him. Mr. Caine, M.P., writing to the " Standard" in reply to some strictures on his attitude towards the Govern- ment on the license purchase proposals of the Govern- ment, says his position as a member of Parliament has always been the same—he supports Government when j they are right and opposes them when they are wrong. Believing, as he does, that large insidious proposals of the Government lay an axe arthe root of the temperance tree, he fights them with the same energy and determina- tion as he fought Home Rule. A London Correspondent says :—Mr. Gladstone's statement on Thursday night that the 'passing of the bill will have the effect of still further inflating the price of public-house property is of great importance, and renders it all the more imperative that there should be a Government valuation of all public-house property in the country before this bill is placed upon the statute- book. The Select Committee of the House of Lords on Intemperance, which reported in 1879, stated that one effect of the changes made by the Act of 1872 in the manner of granting on licenses was to prevent the increase of their number, while the operation of the Act of 1889 had been considerably to decrease the number of beerhouse licenses. The effect of this legislation had been," contiaued the Committee in the course of their report. "to raise the value of .his pro- perty; and it would seem but just that the public should receive a greater portion than hitherto of the profits of a monopoly thus artifically created." The Government are now about still further to increase the monopoly; and it would therefore seem to follow, according to the reason- ing of the Lords' Committee, that this enhancement in the money value of the monopoly ought to be accom- panied by an increase or the Excise license duties. On all hands it is admitted that the value of public-house property is artificially high.

div.head: LOCAL ACTION.
div.p: LOCAL ACTION.

A united lodge meeting of the Good Templars of Warrington was held in the Academy-st. Mission-room, on Wednesday evening, when a resolution condemna- tory of the compensation clauses of the Government licensing bill was passed. Mr. J. H. Lawless occupied the chair, and an address was delivered by Mr. Morris Jones, of Liverpool. A special meeting of the Com- mittee of the Warrington Temperance Federation is to be summoned early next week, for the purpose of con- sidering the compensation clauses of the Bill.

div.head: SCRIPTURE READER'S BIGAMY
div.p: THE SCRIPTURE READER'S BIGAMY
CASE.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, before Mr. Baron Huddleston, James Albert Mason (35), described as an engineer and well-educated, formerly of Golborne, was brought up on a charge of having, at Leeds, feloniously married Annie Clara Taylor, his former wife being still alive. Taylor was unable to be present owing to illness. Pr,soner pleaded guilty, but handed up a letter to his lordship, who read portions of it. The reference, for such it was, stated that prisoner, at that time a Scripture reader, was "a person of Christian character, gentlemanly in appearance. and his heart was all aglow with, love to Christ. lie had been a teacher in a school, and was a thorough devoted Christian, and was likely to prove a real blessing to any parish or district wherever he might be sent.' —His Lordship : I'm afraid the lady who wrote this didn't know your inner lite.— Prisoner said his lordship, would understand the refer- ence if he allowed prisoner to make a statement.— His Lordship : Very well, let me hear your statement.— Prisoner then made a long and profuse statement to the effect that his first wife had been a woman who had a "bad disposition of temper," and led him a terrible life. He therefore left her and married the woman Taylor, but all the time he kept his wife and children by sending them money. He had been a Scripture-reader, and had struggled to lead a godly life, but was dragged down by his first wife. The first year of his life with Taylor was the happiest of his life. His first wife was much ad- dicted to falling from the truth, and she did all she could to annoy him. He had done what he Gould for the best, and had lived an honest godly life with Taylor till the very day he was arrested—His Lordship : This woman says you got 8.140 out of her.—Prisoner; That's not so. my lord. We spent the money in furnishing a lodging- house. She has still got the money, and more I spent myself, represented in that stock.—His Lordship, in pass- ing sentence, said prisoner had no doubt been unhappy in his first marriage, but there was no reason why he should have put Taylor in the position she now occu- pied. However, his case was not a very had one, but he must go to gaol for six months with hard labour.

PENKETH. THE LIBERAL CLUB. The Penketh Liberal Club has recently been very handsomely re-decorated at the expense of Mr. Broadhurst, of Great Sankey. We understand that the Club will shortly be presented with the portrait of Mr. Broa.dhurst's father who was the first presi- dent of the Club. LEorunx y Mn. AND MRS. GARNETT..

On Thursday evening, and last evening, Mr. and Mrs. Garnett, of Penketh, gave descriptive reminis- cence of recent travel in the land of the Pharoahs, to good audiences, in the Penketh Wesleyan School. ' The lectures were illustrated with tableau in Eastern costame. On Thursday evening descriptions i were given of street life n Cairo, visits to the bazaars and mosques' a journey with Stanley's publisher, and a rapid sketch on the outward jour- ney via Marseilles, Genoa, Rome, and Naples to Port Said. Last evening the subjects dealt with were descriptive of three weeks' jcurney on the Nile, the temples and tombs of kings in Upper Egypt. shooting the cataract, boatmen at Assouan, visits to mission schools, end a summary of the re— turn journey from Alexandria to Greece, Corf Venice, Milan, and St. Got hard Pass.

div.p: FRODSIIA.II.

FOOTBALL CLUB ATHLETIC SPORTS.—In connectiom with the Frodsham Football Chib, sports were arranged to take place at Belle Monte, on Saturday. The weather was anything but promising, and this had an effect on the attendance, there being but a limited number of spectators present. Six events were prov,kled, the first being a 120 yards handicap, open. This was run m heats, R. Jones, Widnes, reaching the tape first in the final, the second plate being secured by S. Brimelowt. In the 100 yards handicap, the result of the final was, R. Jones 1* W Chrimes Norley, 2. In the high jump.com- ' petition there Were seven entries. W. Faulkner, Run- corn, who cleared 4ft. CM., was declared the winnerof the prize. Much interest was manifested in the long jump competition. G. H. Tudor, Weston, who cleared 171 t. ho., took the first prize, whilst the second went to W. Faulkner, whose performance was 17ft. The winners of the 120 yards club handicap were P. Hughes, 1, and T.. Tudor, 2. In the 100 yards fiat race, local, G. Webb, Frodsham, came in first, and G. H. Tudor, Weston. second. The judges were Mr. F. T. Parry and Mr. El. Wilcock, whilst Mr. J. Lewis officiated as starter'. Tip Helshy Church and the Frodsharn bands played during the afternoon, and thus enhanced the enjoyment qf the spectators, and an instrumental and vocal concert was given during the evening, the programme consisting rd pianoforte, cornet, and euphonium solos, humourouS and sentimental songs, Mr. C. H. Hibbert presiding at the pianoforte.

Sir G. Trevelyan, addressing a Liberal meeting at Ramsgate, on Wednesday night, accused the Govern- ment of having turned their coat regarding land pur- chase in Ireland, and argued that, having done so, they were now holding office under false pretences. At Edinburgh, on Thursday, a young man named LB. Jamieson, was remanded pending inquiry on a charge of swindling by fraudulent advertisements. The advertise- ments offered lucrative situations in Australia. On Jamieson's house being searched the police fonnd 1,700 letters, 270 of which contained stamps to the value of a shilling fee, which Jamieson, it is alleged, charged. , Other sums were found amountingto £ll. The applies.- ' tions were from all parts of te United Kingdom.
LATEST N E WS.
CRICKET MATCH. Notts innings closed yesterday for 590; Sussex have made thirty for two wickets.

THE CHRISTCHURCH TRAGEDY. At Christchurch yesterday, a married woman named Tremlett, who attempted suicide on Monday, after strangling her youngest daughter, was committed for trial charged with murder.

THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION. At the meeting of the Congregational Union to-day, resolutions were adopted protesting against any attempt to ascertain religious profession during the coming cen- sus, and condemning the liquor traffic with native races.' THE INCE MURDER. At the Liverpool Assizes yesterday, before Baron Hud- (Reston, William Dickinson, collier, and Ann Dickinson, his wife, were indicted for the murder of Hannah Lydia Burchall, aged six years, the daughter of . the female prisoner by a former husband. The body of the child was found in a disused pit shaft near Wigan, murdered and brutally outraged. Prisoners entered a plea of net ' guilty. On the application of counsel for the defence. they were tried separately, the case against the male prisoner being taken first. In the meantime the female prisoner was sent back to the cells. Mr. McConnell. for the prosecution,. described the murder as one of the foulest description prompted by passion and carried out in lust: He then sketched in detail the circum- stances under which the crime was believed to have been committed, and proceeded to call evidence. Wit- nesses spoke to the disappearance of the deceased, and the circumstances under which it took place, and to the ultimate discovery of the body in the Ravine Pit. When evidence to the latter effect had been given the Court adjourned. MR'. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO EAST ANGLIA.

mi:l—alcir-iirs. Gladstone left London yesterday morn- ing for Norwich. They drove from St. James's- square in a Victoria to Lfverpool-st. Station, where a crowd of people-had collected. They cheered the right hon. gentleman heartily as he made his way to the saloon carriageaccompanied by Mr. Colman, Mr. Campbell Bannerman, and others of his party. The train reached Ipswich shortly before noon, and Mr. Gladstone was there accorded a hearty reception from the crowds at the station. Canon Bulstrode read and presented an address from the-combined Liberal Councils of Suffolk, trusting the right hon.. gentleman might be enabled to carry out his efforts to weld together-the United Kingdom by -doing justice to Ireland. Mr. Gladstone expressed his gratification at the terms of the address, and said' the Liberals must never cease to assert that they were the true Unionists. Mr. Gladstone said their opponents were going about the country say- ing nothing could be done for Home Hide until a dissolu- tion. After that it was-possible they might get rid of them; but he was not at all certain they would be any betteroff for it. They mistookthe cause if they thought lit depended' upon individnalS The Government major- ity last night was another sign, of doom hanging over this Parliament. Mr. Gladstone- resumed. his journey amid renewed cheers. Mr. Gladstone arrived in Norwich at oneWelock. The entire population seemed to,have turned out into the streets to greet him, and hisprovress through the city to Carrow House was a triumpher one. The crowds round the station and in Prince of Wales-road, London-street, the Market-place, and Btacondale, were dense. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone acknowledged with evident pleasure the sympathic greetings of the people. The National Liberal Federation Conference was held at Norwich yesterday afternoon. Sir dames Kitson pre. sided, and there was a,large attendance. The Chairman moved a resolution which, he said, embodied the Liberal creed as enunciated at Leeds, Birmingham, and Manches- ter. It welcomed Mt. Gladstone to Norwich and ex- pressed in him unabated confidence.

"PURE FABRICATION."—Lord SOSEMEREY called atten- tion to statements which appeared in an ektract pub- lished in a morning paper yesterday, from the German papers, to the effect that in the summer of 1882, the German Foreign Office peremptorily required England to enter into an offensive and defensive treaty. Lord SALISBURY said the statements were a pure fabrication and without foundation. The Open Spaces 13ildwas read a third time and the House adjourned. HOUSE. OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past two., THE GERMANS IN Areice.—Replying to questions by Sir John Kennaway and Mr. Munro Ferguson, Sir JAMES FERGUSSON added that the Government knew of no action on the part ofthe German Government or Ger- man agents calculatecbto infringe the rights of British subjects in Africa under existing treaties, and that British interests would not suffer by the present discus- sion at Berlin. WRECK OF A LABOUR SCHOONER. _— GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. Advices received at San Francisco tate that the schooner Eliza Mary has been totally wrecked on the coast of the New Hebrides. The schooner had on board a large number of natives, who had been engaged under. the uskal labour contracts to work on the Queensland plantations. Of these no fewer than 47 were drowned, and four white men, forming part of the crew of thl3 vessel, also perished. MASSACRE OF INNOCENTS IN RUSSIA. _— A St. Petersburg correspondent , telegraphing yesterday, says :—lt is believed that some cases of baby-farmioff lately brought to light in Vilna will exceed in horror even those of Warsaw. Hundreds of infants are believed to have been murdered, as, one of the midwives who 11 been arrested confesses that for several .years her oll'e occupation was hiding the dead children m disused wells, canals, forests, &c. Another midwife arrested on ale: picion has attempted to hang herself in her cell, but via' prevented by the gaolers. RAILWAY SERVANTS DEMONSTRATION. A meeting of the Railway Workmen's Union, London, was held on Sunday afternoon, about 10,000 peoPlei being present. There were four platforms, the princiPa speakers being Mr. Cunninghame Graham, M.P., John Burns, Mr. Tom Mann, Mr. Aveling, and Mr. We". son, general secretary of the Union. It was resolved that, the time bad fully arrived when the maximum hours ot railway men in traffic and goods departments be 54 Per week and railway shopmen 51 ; also that railway Mali,9",, gers and directors should at once take steps to gran'. substantial increase to their employes scanty pay. .

SLEEPING OUT.—Frederick Smith, Thomas Leather- barrow, and Catherine Brown were each sent to prison for seven days, with hard labour, for sleeping in a shed at Arpley. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison, and Dr. White. DRUNI(ENNESS.—George McCabe was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-rd., on the previous evening. He was fined ss. and costs. SLEEPING ou.—Alfred Knowles, charged with sleep- ing out at Arpley, the same morning, was sent to prison for fourteen days.—George Cole and John Neil, for sleeping out in a straw-shed at Latchford, were also sent to prison for fourteen days, with hard labour. MAINTENANCE CASES.—On the application of Mr. Shearer, John Frangleton was ordered to pay Is. a week towards the maintenance of his child. James Nicolson and William Nicholson were each ordered to pay is. towards the maintenance of their mother. Joseph Philips consented to pay a similar amount towards the mainten- ance of his mother, and Frederick Hall was ordered to pay ss. towards the maintenance of his father. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CAUL—Several persons were fined for negjecting to send their children regularly to school. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Thomas McGuinness was sum- moned on a charge of having assaulted a young woman named Sarah Cavanagh. Mr. P. Davies appeared for McGuinness and Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins for Cavanagh. After hearing evidence, the Bench decided to bind each of the parties over to keep the peace. WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. P. StObbe. ALLEGED THEFT FROM A FLAT.—Williatll Norman was charged with stealing a quantity of rope from a fiat at Sankey Bridges, between the 6th and Bth of May, the property of John Barton, of Runcorn. The defendant had been engaged to load and unload the fiat. Evidence in support of the charge having been given the case was remanded to the next Warrington County Petty Ses- sions. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. J. MArSOD. RIDING WITHOUT TlCKET.—AlexandraMalcolinson was charged with having travelled from Edgehill to Newton- lctWillows, on the London and North-Western Railway, on the previous day, without having paid his fare. He was remanded.

COLLLERT ACCIDENT IN PENNSYL- VANIA. SUPPOSED LOSS OF 28 LIVES. NEW YORK, FRIDAY MORNING. As stated yesterday, a large portion of a coal mine at Ashley, Pennyslvania, fell in with a fearful crash just after the dinner hoar, and no fewer than 28 men were buried or shut in by the debris. Diver Tonic, FRIDAY NOON.—It is now known that twenty-eight men were entombed in the mine near Ashley, 'Pennsylvania, in consequence of the cave in which occurred yesterday. The strenuous efforts of the rescuers have hitherto resulted in the release of only throe men, all of whom were terrib'y burned. The dis- aster is believed to be due to explosion resulting from the ignition of gas by a miner's lamp. The explosion was so severe that some twenty houses on the surface were shattered, and the inmates were compelled to flee for their lives.
